19-session-liquidity-advanced.summary: A genuinely useful lesson about *when* to trade, built on a four-phase cycle that is easy to hold in the head: Asia builds the range, London sweeps it, New York confirms or rejects, the afternoon fades. fixes: Derek's composite carried the full after-record the corpus rule forbids: '$36,660 → $61,200 (+67%), 43 trades, 35 winners' with an 81% win rate — and it sat four screens above a table whose own header says the win-rate column was removed because the dataset cannot be produced. The caveat beside it did not fix that; it just made the page argue with itself. Replaced with what the checklist demonstrably did: rejected 28 setups he would previously have taken, with no way to know how those would have gone.

'ANY rule prevents 5-8 losses, ALL rules = $0 lost' is a backtest fitted to the same twelve trades it was derived from — exactly the overfitting the curriculum warns about elsewhere. Kept the counts, added the admission: the rules were written after looking at these twelve losses, so of course they catch these twelve, which makes them a hypothesis to test forward rather than a result.

The NQ worked example ended with a constructed outcome ('dropped 15,480 → 15,310 over next 6 hours, 170-point move'). The ES example above it states no outcome at all, so the pair was inconsistent as well as invented. Replaced with the sequence the example actually teaches — divergence, then structure break, then entry with the stop above the failed high — and the note that no worked example can tell you whether a given one followed through, which is why there is a stop.

The delta interpretation bands (+1000 = strong, ±300 = balanced) were given with no instrument or timeframe attached, so a reader would apply ES 5-minute numbers to a 1-minute chart or a stock. Added the scaling note: +1000 is enormous on a bar that trades 2,000 contracts and unremarkable on one that trades 40,000, so calibrate the bands to what a typical bar in your instrument actually prints.

Two direct contradictions inside the flagship example. The footprint table labelled the +2,100 row '🔥 STRONG BUY' while the surrounding prose calls that same level a trap and 'light buying at top' — relabelled 'Aggressive buying', which is what the numbers show without endorsing it, and rewrote the prose to compare the two sides in contracts (5,900 hit the bid below, 3,700 lifted the offer above) so the reader can check it.

The pattern table's Reliability column read 'Low' on both exhaustion rows while the same rows recommend a fade — ambiguous about what is low. Now 'Low as a bullish signal' and 'Low as a bearish signal'.
20-footprint-charts-advanced.summary: The best on-ramp in the corpus. A reader who has never seen a footprint chart gets a 30-second explainer, a side-by-side 'same bar, two stories' comparison, and then a worked footprint table whose arithmetic is exact — the five per-level deltas sum to the stated -1,400 and the five level volumes sum to the stated 11,800. That internal consistency is rare and it is what makes the trap example land. Parts 2-4 build cleanly: imbalance → stacked imbalance → absorption vs exhaustion (with the four-way context grid that is the real content of the lesson) → POC migration → divergence. The nine-row pattern table at the end is a genuine reference. Both worked examples state entry, stop and targets before anything else. At 4,097 words this is the longest beginner lesson and it earns the length. The residual weakness is that reliability ratings across the nine-row table are editorial judgements presented in a column that looks measured; the table's own header now says no win rates are claimed, which is the honest framing available. Derek's loss record (12 trades, 0 winners, -$28,340, and the three named losers) stays: a composite may illustrate a mistake. The 'trust the footprint — not because it is never wrong' line stays as one of the better caveats in the corpus.
20-footprint-charts-advanced.title: Footprint Charts: Reading Institutional Intent

fixes: The Marcus-versus-Aisha comparison was the corpus's worst constructed win: two invented traders, same stock, same three weeks, with a stated '$8,170 performance gap', Marcus at 0 wins from 3 and Aisha at 2 from 2 — presented as proof that 'understanding institutional behavior is the entire edge', four screens from a table that says its win-rate columns were removed because the dataset cannot be shown. Rewritten to keep the pedagogy and drop the scoreboard: each side now describes where its rules take it, and the closing note says outright that a composite can be written so whichever side the author prefers comes out ahead, and names the four decisions where the approaches actually diverge.

Twenty-one blocks of dead .quiz-feedback markup across nine lessons (20, 56, 57, 58, 59, 60, 61, 75, 78). 21-swing-trading-framework.summary: The tier's closing lesson and the one that carries the most weight: it has to convince a reader who has spent nineteen lessons on intraday mechanics that the daily chart is a different game, and it does. The scaling arithmetic is exact — the SPY average entry of $592.20 and the TSLA 2.96R both check out to the cent. Two quiz blocks totalling eight questions is still more than any other lesson, but with the celebration moved to the end the order at least reads correctly. fixes: Nina's composite still carried a recovery arc — a 'Final $142K' stat box and 'Account recovered $83K → $142K in 5 months' in the case-study answer. Removed. The answer now says what the fix removes (a cost paid 18 times a day whether she was right or wrong) rather than what it earned.

'Limit orders only — roughly 60% of the spread saved' was an efficacy figure with nothing behind it, repeated in the quiz explanation. Replaced with the mechanism: on a limit order she is quoting rather than paying, so the spread stops being a cost charged at every entry.

The practice exercise was confirmation bias by design. Its success metric was 'find 3-5 instances where spread widening preceded price movement', which can only ever confirm the signal. Rewritten to demand a count rather than a collection: log every widening including the ones followed by nothing, two columns, and finish able to say 'N times, M of them moved'. The note that a signal firing eleven times and preceding a move four times is still useful — but only if you know it is four out of eleven — is the point the exercise now teaches.

Replaced with what is actually happening (a market maker repricing risk, often before the risk reaches price) plus the failure modes the exercise then makes the reader count: a quote server hiccup, one participant stepping away, the tail of an auction.

22-bid-ask-spread-dynamics.summary: The best-argued lesson in the corpus so far, and the one whose arithmetic holds up under the closest reading. Its central move is to convert an invisible cost into a break-even win rate the reader can check: a 1-point stop with a 0.25-point spread needs 62.5% at 1:1, and the lesson says 63%; Nina's $25 spread against a $75 stop needs 66.7%, and the lesson says 67%. Both derivations are correct, and both are the kind of number a reader can verify with a pen. The internal consistency of the composite is equally rare: 1,620 trades at $25 is $40,500, quoted as $41K; week 8's 90 trades at $25 is exactly the $2,250 stated. The reframing of the spread as a tax on impatience rather than a fee, and of market makers as being paid for your urgency, is the clearest explanation of microstructure cost in the curriculum. The only remaining soft spot is the Step 3 table mapping spread width to a maximum number of trades per day; those counts are editorial judgement presented in the same visual register as the derived arithmetic elsewhere on the page. Nina's disaster record (1,620 trades, 61%, -$41K gross and -$41K in spread, $165K → $83K) stays, and so does the sentence that makes it land: the spread did not turn a winner into a loser, it doubled a loser. The <10%-of-stop rule stays, now labelled a rule of thumb, because the lesson derives the real break-even arithmetic beside it.
22-bid-ask-spread-dynamics.title: The Spread is Stealing From You (And You Don't Even Notice)

strengths: The ratio explains the trap it is built on: the instruments that look most attractive on a chart are the ones whose spreads widen faster than their ranges, and those two facts have the same cause.
Refuses to stop at the ranking. Lowest friction is a shortlist, not a decision; the instrument must also produce the behaviour the method exploits and trade when the reader is awake.
The minimum-account arithmetic names the real failure mode -- traders shrink the stop rather than change instrument, then conclude the method does not work.
The quiz explanation for Q1 attacks the plausible principle that costs and ranges scale together, which is exactly why neither number alone will do.
23-what-should-you-trade.summary: New lesson answering the first real decision a trader makes, which the curriculum had never addressed: instrument selection appeared twice in 82 lessons. The artefact is the friction ratio -- round-trip cost divided by average daily range, both in basis points -- which turns 'what should I trade' into a ranked list the reader produces from their own broker's quotes in an evening. Mega-cap tech gives up about 1% of its daily range to friction; a $1.50 micro-cap gives up 73%.
23-what-should-you-trade.title: What Should You Actually Trade?

Rewritten to a tally: every logged wall goes into exactly one of three columns, and the proportions across all ten or more are the output. Collecting only the interesting walls measures nothing.
'Result: High-probability long setup' in the imbalance section, in a lesson whose whole argument is that no single order book reading is worth acting on alone.
25-order-book-analysis.summary: The single most useful distinction in the microstructure sequence, taught cleanly: the order book shows intentions, which can be cancelled, and only a tested level shows anything real. Everything downstream follows from that — absorption versus exhaustion as the same setup with opposite outcomes, the three iceberg detection methods (refreshing, volume exceeding visible size, price stickiness), and spoofing identified by what a fake wall does rather than by how big it is. Jake's disaster is the best-constructed cautionary record in the corpus: three phases summing exactly to the stated -$72,000, running balances that reconcile at every step ($165K → $136.6K → $104.7K → $93K), and 34 trades with 6 wins matching the quoted 17%. The 'absorbs 5,000+ shares = real' threshold is instrument-specific and stated flatly; it works as a rule of thumb for the liquid names the lesson uses but would mislead on a thin one. Worth a scale note if this lesson is revisited, of the kind added to lesson 19's delta bands. Jake's disaster half stays in full — the three named trades, the per-phase win rates (21%, 17%, 13%), the running balances, and his journal entry, which is the most honest paragraph in the case study. His closing advice stays under a heading that no longer calls it a transformation.
25-order-book-analysis.title: The Order Book is Theater (Here's What's Real)

fixes: 'Real Example: Tesla Stop Hunt (September 2024)' was the corpus's most serious fabrication: a minute-by-minute account with timestamps, share counts and low prints, presented as a recorded event, on a date when TSLA was not trading anywhere near the quoted $242. Relabelled as an illustrative reconstruction, the date and ticker attribution removed, and the reader told directly to treat any minute-by-minute account of a sweep — here or anywhere else — as a diagram rather than as evidence.

Inside that example, two invented figures derived from the invented data: '~$15-20M of stop liquidity based on volume profile' and 'estimated profit for hunt orchestrators: $125K-$420K in 45 minutes'. The first is replaced with the honest statement that stop liquidity is unknowable from outside — which is exactly why it is worth so much to whoever can see it — and the second with the economic point that survives without numbers: the buyer is buying from people who are not choosing to sell.

'How Janus Atlas users traded this: Result: +1.1% gain while stopped-out traders lost -1%' — a product efficacy claim built on a fabricated tape. Replaced with the setup's actual content: where the entry sits, where the stop sits, and $1.40 per share at risk at a level that has just proven it can be broken.

'The pattern repeats every single day across thousands of instruments' — replaced with the version that is true and more useful: common enough to learn, not a rule, and plenty of breaks below support are just breaks below support. Janus Atlas marks the sweeps; it cannot tell you which reverse, which is why the entry waits for the reclaim.

'Stop hunts aren't manipulation—they're automated liquidity provision' is a legal characterisation the lesson is not in a position to make, and it sits oddly beside the same lesson's 'dirty tricks' and 'maximum carnage'. Now: whether a given sweep crosses that line is for a regulator with the order records; what matters to you is that none of it is aimed at you personally and all of it is aimed at where predictable stops sit.
'Total liquidity: $10M+ in guaranteed sell orders' — stops are not guaranteed anything, as lesson 20 spends a section establishing. Now 'a pool of forced sell orders — not chosen, just triggered'.

Two slippage figures stated as results ('$0.08 → $0.01/share', repeated in the quiz). Replaced with the structural fact: a limit order cannot fill worse than its limit, so the slippage line goes to nothing on the fills you get and the cost moves to the fills you don't.

An after-record hiding inside the case-study answer, which the earlier corpus sweep missed because it was mid-paragraph: 'Results: stop hunt rate 12/month → 1/month, recovered +$51K.' Removed, with the observation that replaces it — three of the four rebuild rules make his stop harder to find and none make him faster.
26-market-making-hft.summary: The lesson that reframes the whole microstructure sequence: you are not being cheated, you are being modelled, and the fix is not speed. Part 1 is its best work — three revenue streams with the arithmetic shown ($0.05 × 1M shares × 250 days = $12.5M; $0.0015 rebate × 1M × 250 = $375K), which converts an abstraction into a business you can see yourself funding. The stop-hunt economics in Part 3 are the clearest statement in the corpus of why stops cluster where they do and why that clustering is worth money to someone. Carlos's disaster reconciles exactly: $68,200 in hunts at ~$1,450 across 47 events, plus $5,800 of slippage, equals the stated $74,000, and $155K less that is the stated $81K. Evidence graded B rather than A: the lesson's factual spine (rebate economics, co-location, IEX's speed bump) is sound, but the '~50% of US equity volume' figure and the maker-taker rates are quoted without a source. That framing does more in one screen than most lessons do in a section, and everything after it is downstream of a question the reader now genuinely wants answered. The six-loss autopsy is the strongest part of the case study and survives the audit intact: each loss names the textbook pattern and the delta that contradicted it, six times out of six, which is a checkable correspondence rather than a claim about returns. fixes: The lit-versus-dark comparison had a million shares filling in a single print at the midpoint within six seconds. That is not how a dark pool works, and it makes the venue sound like a magic fill button — a claim lesson 65 spends its length contradicting. Rewritten: the pool matches whatever finds a willing counterparty, in pieces, over hours or days; a real order of that size is worked across several venues, some of it lit, and still moves the price. What the pool removes is the advertising, not the impact.

Three constructed wins, each attached to a specific month and each ending in a rally: TSLA to $253.80, NVDA to $938, SPY to $545.80. All three replaced with what the example is actually for — the read, the score, or the confluence — plus, in the first case, the instruction to ask how a lesson knows an outcome it claims.

The 'Silent Accumulation' case study ended with a fabricated day-3 result. Replaced with what you would be watching for, and the note that sometimes the accumulation simply stops, which is why this is a reason to watch rather than a reason to be positioned.

Jennifer's composite carried a '+$136K recovered' after-record. Removed. What replaces it is the thing the rule actually gives her: a way to notice the flow has rotated — which is what she could not see in 2023 and the reason her 2022 results were not what she thought they were.

Four probability claims: 'Expected performance: High probability (extreme confluence)', 'high-probability short setup', 'Highest probability setup' as the label on the 5-7 point band, and 'one of the highest-probability long setups in order flow trading' in the quiz. Each replaced with a statement about the evidence — how many independent things had to agree — and, in the quiz, with the reminder that extreme confluence is not the same as certainty, which is why there is a stop.

The venue table attributed Goldman's Sigma X and Morgan Stanley's MS Pool to a single row labelled '(Goldman)'. Corrected, and the 'Signal Strength' column renamed to what it actually is: how much weight to give it.

The defended-cost-basis argument is legitimate, but so is the opposite: institutions carrying a losing position at $186 are exactly the people who sell into a bounce to $186. The teaser for lesson 26 said 'Price can be manipulated. Order flow can't' — which lesson 22 spends a whole section refuting, since spoofing is order flow. Replaced with what is true: pushing price for a moment is cheap, executed volume is not, because it has to be paid for.
28-dark-pools.summary: The best-sourced lesson in the intermediate tier: it points the reader at data they can actually get for free (FINRA TRF, DIX at squeezemetrics.com, Quiver Quant) and at a specific tell they can verify themselves — midpoint execution with no order-book footprint. The four print characteristics are a genuine identification procedure rather than a vibe. The three-filter system with its 7-point scoring is the most disciplined framework in the corpus so far, and it already carried the right caveat about not quoting the win rate it produces. The 'Limitations (Be Honest)' section, which concedes the data is delayed and that a single print can be rebalancing or hedging, is the kind of section most lessons in this corpus needed and did not have. The opening's 'roughly two fifths, depending on whose count you use' is the right hedge for a figure that varies by definition — it survives unchanged. Also extended sanity.py's Turkish allowlist with 'parça parça' and 'azar azar', both legitimate reduplications of the same class as the entries already there. Jennifer's seven losing trades and the two named examples. The DIX bands, which come from a named free source. The three-filter system and the scoring, whose point totals reconcile with their bands, and which already declined to quote a win rate.
28-dark-pools.title: They're Buying in the Dark (But You Can See the Footprints)

fixes: The lesson contradicted itself on its own premise. The Real Talk box said 'order flow can't be faked', the page title and all three social meta descriptions said 'Price can be manipulated. Three counterfactual savings: 'Saved -$1,140 (bounced hard)' on a skipped trade, 'Skipped 2 trades that would have lost $2,080', and 'Skipped 4 false breakouts (saved $3,840 in losses)'. A trade not taken has no outcome. The skipped-trade cell now reads 'No trade, so no result', and the metrics list says the cost or saving is unknowable and that any lesson putting a number on one is inventing it.

'War Story: SPY's Fake Break at $450' was a fabricated event with a date, ending in an 8R win. Relabelled illustrative, the outcome removed, and replaced with the part that actually teaches: thirty cents of risk between entry and stop, and the fact that a slowdown and an exhaustion look identical until one of them stops.

Five probability and expectancy claims: 'Reversal UP (high probability)' and its bearish twin, 'Triple Divergence Reversal (High Expectancy)', 'Expected performance: High probability (extreme confluence)', 'stack for highest probability' in the takeaways, and 'highest-probability reversal setup' in the quiz. Each replaced with a statement about evidence rather than odds — and the triple-divergence section now says plainly why it is rare (five conditions at once) and points at where its stop sits.

'Who wins? The money. Every time.' Replaced with the honest version: usually the better-informed side is the one that can afford patience, which is not the same as the side that is right — institutions bought all the way down through 2008 too.
'You now see markets the way hedge funds do' — replaced with what the reader can actually now do: ask whether a new high was paid for, and wait for a trigger before acting on the answer.
29-smart-money-divergence.summary: A well-organised lesson with one genuinely excellent section that most of the corpus lacks: 'Common Divergence Mistakes' concedes, unprompted, that a single divergence can persist for weeks in a strong trend, that divergences against the higher-timeframe trend usually produce consolidation rather than reversal, and that a divergence without a trigger is an invitation to sit in drawdown. That is three real limitations stated plainly, and it is why the framework that follows — minimum two divergences, plus a structural trigger — is worth following. The four divergence types are cleanly separated by what data each one reads, and the quiz arithmetic checks out (120K→50K is the stated 58%, +8,500→+2,000 the stated 76%). Two different average-loss figures appear for two different subsets ($1,140 across the three worked examples, $1,036 across all eleven). Both are correct arithmetic for their own set but sitting close together they read like an inconsistency; left as is since fixing it would mean inventing detail for the other eight trades. Tyler's eleven losses and the three worked-out examples, which are the argument: in each one the divergence was visible before he entered, and each is checkable against its own description. The 'Common Divergence Mistakes' section untouched — it was already doing the job the rest of the lesson needed.
29-smart-money-divergence.title: When Price Lies, Follow the Money

fixes: The practice exercise ended: 'After 10 trades, compare expectancy of 3/3 alignment vs 1/3 alignment. The data will prove the framework works.' That is an exercise designed to confirm its own lesson, at a sample size that cannot settle anything, scoring only the trades the reader took. Rewritten with both problems named: ten trades will be mostly noise, and if you only score what you entered you have thrown away the comparison group — so log the 1/3 setups you skipped and what they did.

'Real Trade Example: SPY Long Setup — Trade Setup: March 15, 2024' ended in a win ('SPY rallied to $517.80 by next day, target hit, 3.53R'). Relabelled as a worked example with illustrative prices, the outcome removed, and replaced with what the five steps actually produce: three levels each chosen by the timeframe that can see it, and a risk-reward you know before you click.
Alex's composite carried a 'Final $315K' balance beside the $350K start and $223K trough. Removed; the disaster and the trough stay, and his own quote already declined to give a new win rate.

Seven probability claims. The three alignment tiers were labelled 'Highest / Moderate / Low probability' — the ordering is right but the units were wrong, so each now describes how many independent readings agree. Also fixed: 'highest probability setups' in the intro, 'Perfect alignment = highest probability / optimal expectancy' in the takeaways, 'Highest conviction trades (optimal expectancy)' in the Omnideck section, and 'highest probability setup' in the quiz answer.

The quiz answer 'Adding more timeframes creates analysis paralysis. 3 timeframes is optimal' asserted optimality; it now gives the reason — the 15-minute has already answered the timing question, so a fourth opinion adds noise rather than evidence.
30-multi-timeframe-mastery.summary: The most cleanly structured lesson in the tier. The core idea — HTF for bias, MTF for structure, LTF for timing, and never let a timeframe do a job it cannot see — is stated once and then held consistently through a four-step workflow, a five-step execution table, three alignment tiers, a scaling-in ladder and a scaling-out ladder. The arithmetic is exact throughout: the worked SPY setup's $5.50 over $1.50 is the stated 3.67R, and the pyramid's weighted average entry (50% at $512.50, 25% at $514.20, 25% at $516.50) is the stated $513.90 to the cent. Alex's disaster is the right kind of composite: the failure mode is named as blindness rather than bad luck, and the quote admits the prior year's success was accidental alignment with a trend he did not know existed. The three alignment tiers now describe evidence rather than odds, but they still rank setups, which is the correct thing for this framework to do — three independent readings agreeing genuinely is more evidence than one. The change is that the lesson no longer converts that into an implied hit rate. Alex's record in full (87 trades, 31%, -$127,000, the three named losses, and the admission that 2023's +$94K was luck). His closing line, which already refused to quote a post-fix win rate off five months, is one of the better caveats in the corpus and needed no change.
30-multi-timeframe-mastery.title: Single Timeframe Trading = Gambling

fixes: 'This setup has 75-80% win rate historically' — the most explicit fabricated statistic found in the audit so far, sitting in a quiz answer. Removed and replaced with the reason it cannot be quoted: nobody has measured this setup across a sample worth the name, and a figure invented for a lesson is worse than no figure. What survives is the checkable part — four independent things had to agree, and if the stop goes they were all wrong together.

The three framework-ranking sentences were each attached to the block BEFORE the framework they describe: 'Why this one ranks highest' sat under Multi-Timeframe Confluence but describes Sweep-and-Reclaim, and both 'Where it stands' paragraphs were one block early. All three moved into the framework they belong to. Pure relocation, so no retranslation cost.

The 'missed profits' accounting — '$94.6K missed', '$127K swing', '$158.6K swing', repeated in three places — assumed Jordan would have held every one of those moves to the end. That is the assumption a stopped-out trader most wants to make and the least able to justify. Removed everywhere, with the distinction stated plainly: the $64K is what happened, the rest is what he tells himself happened.

The recovery record ('23 trades, 18 winners, $44K → $89.6K, +104%') and the Pareto claim in his own quote ('20% of setups = 80% profits'). Both gone. What replaces them is the one measurable change: 23 entries where there had been 54, a 60% cut — and the observation that all four new rules subtract entries rather than improving them, which is the whole mechanism.

Nine probability claims: 'Double sweeps are highest probability setups' in the Real Talk and in all three social meta descriptions, 'Pattern #1 (Highest Probability)' as a heading, 'strong absorption (high probability)', 'Expected performance: Moderate to high probability' twice, 'High probability reversal', 'Extreme reversal probability', 'Highest-conviction long setup', and the takeaway calling the double sweep 'the highest-probability pattern'. Each replaced with what is actually observable — how many layers of stops were cleared, or how many independent readings agreed.
'clears 4H + 15m stops = $50M+ institutional flow' — an invented dollar figure for something not visible from outside. Replaced with the statement that no figure can honestly be put on it.

Two sections titled '⚡ Quick Wins for Tomorrow' in one lesson. The second is a review exercise, not a quick win, and the lesson had no practice section at all — retitled 'Practice: Classify Last Week's Sweeps'.

'You now know patterns that hedge funds use daily' — replaced with the actual takeaway, which is smaller and more useful: being early to a real reversal and being wrong look identical for the first thirty minutes.
31-janus-atlas-advanced.summary: The double-sweep idea is genuinely worth the lesson: the first sweep takes the obvious stops, the bounce creates a new layer of them, and the second sweep takes both — which explains why a trader can be right about the level and still be stopped out twice before the move. Jordan's case study is unusually good at making that concrete, because the failure is not 'he was wrong', it is 'he was early in a specific, repeatable way, 47 times out of 54'. The three execution frameworks are correctly ranked by how much confirmation each demands, and the 'Common Janus Mistakes' section concedes that not all sweeps reverse. The internal inconsistency between '$32.8K losses' in his quote and '-$64K' in the header disappeared with the missed-profits arithmetic that produced it. Also required rebuilding HTF/LTF acronyms across all eleven locales after the splice, and correcting a Japanese myriad-grouping artefact where 6万4千 tokenises as 60004. Jordan's disaster in full: 54 trades, 7 winners, -$64K, the 47-of-54 pattern, and the three named examples with their entries and stops. The 87% figure stays because it describes the shape of his losses, not the value of a method.
31-janus-atlas-advanced.title: Beyond Basic Sweeps: The Double Sweep Power Move

fixes: A genuine arithmetic error in the composite's own results box: '-$37,050 (10 losses)'. The twelve listed trades carry $39,950 of losses, and $39,950 minus the $5,600 of wins is exactly the -$34,350 net stated two boxes above. Corrected to -$39,950, which now reconciles both ways.

Five overlapping counterfactual savings figures — 'Saved: $19,850 / $15,750 / $11,300 / $31,650 / $4,200' — and the heading that totalled them, 'Circuit Breaker Rules Brandon Violated (And How They Would Have Saved $31,650)'. Brandon's entire recovery record: the paper-trading week that supposedly produced '71% win rate' for 3/3 confluence and '28%' for 1/3 or 2/3 (one week of paper trades cannot produce either number), the live return of '8 trades, won 6 (75% win rate), recovered $4,800 (+15.7%)', and 'By June, he had recovered $18,500 of the $34K loss'. What replaces them is the measurable part — 8 trades where the previous three weeks produced 12, and a position-size trigger set at 20 rule-following trades rather than a profit target.

Four fabricated win rates in the quiz explanations and the practice section: 'textbook POC magnet trade with 65-70% win rate', 'CVD divergence + LVN = 60-70% reversal probability', 'Works 70%+ in ranging/choppy conditions', and the Pro insight's '65-70% hold rate' versus '50-50 hold/break'. Each is now a statement about what the confluence is and what would falsify it. The Pro insight in particular becomes more useful, not less: the two regimes are still described, but as two different situations to identify rather than two hold rates to quote.

Five probability labels — two 'Expected performance: High probability' headers, 'High probability support', 'Highest probability support', and 'Why this was the highest-probability trade of the week' — reframed as what has to line up, or how many independent readings agreed.

The weekly return headline '23.1% in that one week'. The +$5,775 stays, because it is simply the seven journal trades added together and the reader can check it; a 23.1% weekly return is an efficacy claim wearing an arithmetic costume.

'This is professional-grade order flow analysis. Most traders trade blind. You now see where institutions positioned.' — replaced with the actual distinction the lesson teaches: volume profile answers where the trading happened, which is a different question from where the price went.

The closing takeaway's 'Jordan's $5,775 profit came from reading the PATTERN', which attributed a week's dollar result to the method. Replaced with the sharper comparison already implicit in the material: Jordan's losing Wednesday still reads as a correctly-executed trade in his own journal, and Brandon's two winners do not read as anything he could repeat.
32-plutus-flow-mastery.summary: The central distinction is a real one and the lesson is built entirely around it: a POC level is a static snapshot, POC migration is a direction, and reading the first while ignoring the second is what separates the two composites. Jordan's five-day journal is the strongest piece of evidence in the intermediate tier so far — every trade's R and dollar figure reconciles exactly against the stated variable risk (2% for A-grade, 1% for the single B-grade loser), so a reader who checks the arithmetic finds it holds, including on the losing Wednesday. Brandon's twelve-trade disaster is genuinely diagnostic rather than cautionary decoration: each loss maps onto a specific misreading, and the five rules that follow are stated as things that remove entries. This lesson had the densest concentration of invented statistics found in the audit so far: nine fabricated rates and five counterfactual dollar figures on one page, alongside a case study whose own arithmetic is exact. The two coexisting is the pattern the whole audit keeps finding — the careful work and the invented work sit in the same document, and the invented parts are always the ones making a claim about how well the method pays. Brandon's disaster in full — 12 trades, 2 wins, -$34,350, -52.8% of a $65,000 account, and the per-trade losses that now sum correctly. Jordan's seven-trade journal with every entry, exit, stop and R value, and the caveats already sitting around it ('Seven trades cannot tell you a win rate', 'Six winners, one loser — a week, not a win rate'), which are among the best-written in the corpus.
32-plutus-flow-mastery.title: Plutus Flow Mastery: Volume Profile & Delta Precision

fixes: The full before→after arc around Marcus. The winning streak ('68 trades, 58% WR, +$42,300, +56.4%') and the recovery ('33/52 wins, 63% WR, +$18,900, +60%, $31.5K → $50.4K') both removed. The streak now says he traded breakouts for eight months and they worked, with a note that no figure is given because the point is that he drew the wrong conclusion from it — and a bigger number would only make the wrong conclusion look better founded. The rule that fixed him stays; what replaces its results is the mechanism, which is visible without them.

'Win rate 58% → 24%' did not reconcile with the trades listed beneath it in either direction: the 58% came from the deleted streak, and the disaster's own counts are 9 wins in 44 trades, which is 20%. The rest of the disaster arithmetic is exact and stays: 3W/16L, 6W/19L, one NVDA loss, -$11,200 -$12,800 -$19,550 = -$43,550, which is 58.1% of $75,000 and leaves the $31.5K stated.

Seven fabricated performance figures: 'Expected performance: 65-75%' and '60-70%' in Part 1, and in the Key Takeaways 'Expected win rate: 58-65% / Avg R:R 1:2.5', '62-70% / 1:1.4', and '38-45% if you trade'. Each replaced with the shape of the trade the regime rewards — few large winners against many small ones — which is the thing the lesson actually teaches and the thing that does not need a dataset.

'Real-world data proves regime matters more than strategy', with 'Same trader: +15% in trending, +5% in ranging, -12% in volatile' and '80% of annual profits come from trending regimes'.
