'Trader A' in the SPY January 2024 example carried invented profits (+$4,200 and +$3,800) against Trader B's -$6,400. The profits are gone and the loss stays, with the asymmetry explained in the block: you can see exactly why B's three shorts were stopped, because SPY went to 510; what A would have made is a guess, and a guess in the profitable direction is the one to distrust.

A factual error in the BTC example: 'May 12, 2021: China announces mining crackdown'. May 12 was Tesla suspending bitcoin payments; China's State Council statement came on May 21. Corrected, with the second catalyst noted in its right place.

Two confirmation-bias prompts in Quick Wins: 'You'll likely find 60%+ of losses came from regime mismatch' (telling the reader the answer before they count) and 'This one habit will eliminate 30% of bad trades'. Both now point at the reader's own log without predicting what it will say.

'Weekly review: Win rate 55-70% if matched, <45% if mismatched' in the framework box — replaced with the instruction to count matched and mismatched trades separately, which is the split that makes the review worth doing.

Two 'Historical observations' hedges that gestured at evidence without having any ('This pattern has shown consistency in trending markets when properly identified'). Replaced with why the pieces are arranged as they are: the trend gives direction, the HTF level gives a place to be wrong, and the absorption is what distinguishes a bought pullback from a pausing one.
33-volume-oracle-regimes.summary: The premise is one of the few in the corpus that survives contact with reality: a strategy is not a thing that works or doesn't, it is a thing that fits some conditions and not others, and 'my strategy stopped working' almost always means the conditions changed. The lesson is structured well around that — three regimes, four detection inputs with numeric thresholds a reader can actually check on a chart (ADX 20/25, VIX 25, ATR 3-5x), and a strategy for each. The five 'Regime Blindness Patterns' are the strongest section: each is a symptom the reader can recognise in their own behaviour, paired with a cause and a specific instruction, and PATTERN 5 ('I'm a breakout trader') correctly identifies the identity trap underneath the whole failure mode. Nine of this lesson's numbers were invented and its single hardest fact — Marcus's loss — reconciles exactly. The pattern holds: the fabrications cluster on claims about how well the method pays, never on the arithmetic of how it fails. Marcus's disaster in full, including the escalation that makes it useful — increasing size to 'make back' in February and removing the stop on the March NVDA trade. Trader D's -68% in the BTC example and Trader B's -$6,400 in the SPY example. All four detection thresholds. The 'What Each Regime Rewards' block, which an earlier pass had already rewritten to explain the mechanism after deleting a fabricated table, and which is now the model the rest of the lesson matches.
33-volume-oracle-regimes.title: Volume Oracle: Stop Fighting the Market's Mood

fixes: Rachel's disaster was dated to Feb 5, 2024, a real session that did not do what the story needs it to do — the Nasdaq closed roughly flat that day. Same defect as the Tesla stop hunt in lesson 23. The date is gone, with the reason stated in the text: she is a composite, and pinning a composite to a real session invites the reader to look it up and find a day that did not do this.

The recovery record, 'Results: 61% win rate, +$14,800, max DD 4.2% (vs 12%)', and its echo in the takeaways, 'Recovery: +$14.8K (19.8% gain) with proper diversification'. The stress test around it survives, because a modelled loss computed from a stated allocation is a calculation the reader can redo; a six-month return is not. The text now says which of the two it is.

The takeaway heading 'Real-world case studies prove the pattern' — Rachel is explicitly labelled a composite four paragraphs above it. Replaced with 'The failure mode is the evidence, and it is arithmetic', and the bullet under it now shows the arithmetic: 8 positions at 1.5% is 12% heat, and 12% is exactly what she lost.

'Even A-grade setups fail 30-40% of the time' — an invented failure rate doing real work in the argument. Replaced with the point it was there to make: A-grade setups fail often enough that several failing on the same day is ordinary, and five of them is 10% heat on that ordinary day.

Two absolute claims: 'This rule alone will prevent catastrophic drawdowns' and 'Keep portfolio heat at 6-8% ... to survive black swan events'. Both now say what the cap actually does rather than promising survival.

'Real Example: Monthly Rebalancing in Action' retitled 'Worked Example' — it is a constructed illustration, not a real account. Its numbers stay untouched, because they are checkable: 38% x 15% = 5.7%, 30% x 15% = 4.5%, and the 1.2% difference is $1,200 on $100K.

The closing line 'Professionals survive market crashes' — replaced with what the lesson actually establishes: the difference shows up on the one day a year when every position turns out to have been the same position.
34-portfolio-construction.summary: This is one of the most useful lessons in the tier, because the thing it teaches is arithmetic and the arithmetic is right. Four positions at 2% risk is 8% total only if they are four different bets; if they all move together it is one 8% bet wearing four names, and a reader who takes nothing else away has still learned something that will change what they do. The 6-8% heat rule is stated as a cap on what being wrong all at once costs, not as a way of being right more often. The correlation section gives the reader a method rather than a rule of thumb — export 30 days of closes, compute daily returns, run CORREL(), colour the matrix — which is unusually concrete for this curriculum, and the reference pairs (SPY/QQQ 0.95, SPY/Gold 0.10-0.30, SPY/VIX -0.80) are close enough to right that a reader who checks them will find the method works. Graded S on 'worth the time' — this is the lesson most likely to change a reader's behaviour on the day they read it, because the failure it describes is one nearly every retail trader has had and almost none has named. The defects were confined to the composite's outcomes and one invented failure rate; the load-bearing arithmetic was already sound throughout. Rachel's disaster in full and its arithmetic, which reconciles exactly: 8 positions, 1.5% each, 12% heat, -$10,200 on $85,000 is -12%, and $85,000 - $10,200 = the $74,800 stated. The stress test on the rebuilt portfolio, relabelled as the calculation it is. The Kelly section's expectancy worked examples, whose arithmetic also checks out (0.6x3 - 0.4x1 = +1.4R; 0.5x2 - 0.5x1 = +0.5R) and which correctly insists that neither win rate nor payoff ratio alone is edge. The quiz explanation's 8 x 1.75% = 14%.
34-portfolio-construction.title: Portfolio Construction: Why All Your Trades Blow Up at Once

fixes: The practice exercise instructed readers to 'use the validation scorecard from the template (8 categories, 60 points max)' and to score 50-60 to proceed. No such scorecard existed anywhere on the site — the phrase appears nowhere else in the codebase. The lesson's single most actionable step pointed at nothing. Built the scorecard from the eight checks the lesson already teaches (data split, optimisation restraint, cost modelling, look-ahead, out-of-sample degradation, walk-forward consistency, sample size, breadth), each scored 0-5 for 40 points, with thresholds. Chris's strategy scores 2 out of 40 on it, which is stated, and is the point.

Expectancy and Sharpe thresholds miscalibrated upward throughout, in a lesson whose entire subject is miscalibration. The red flag list warned only above +5R expectancy; a quiz called a +1.2R expectancy 'still profitable but barely'; another prescribed trading live only if expectancy stayed above +1.5R; a third called Sharpe 1.5-2.5 'realistic'. Taken together these tell a reader that a genuinely excellent system is marginal. Recalibrated: above +0.5R needs an explanation, above +1R almost always means a broken execution assumption — and the lesson now points at its own case study, whose 'holy grail' backtest was +1.3R, to make the point stick.

'Why 90% of backtests fail when taken live' — an invented statistic in the opening promise. Replaced with the claim the lesson actually proves: a backtest can be arithmetically correct and still describe a strategy nobody can trade.

Three unsourced magnitudes: 'your backtest is probably 20-40% too optimistic', 'survivorship bias inflates backtest results by 20-50%', and 'excluding 200+ stocks that got delisted/bankrupted'. The last is also wrong on the facts — index turnover is real but most departures are acquisitions or size-band exits, not bankruptcies. All three now describe the mechanism and its direction and hand the magnitude back to the reader's own calculation, which is what the rest of the lesson demands anyway.

The fantasy backtest's headline, '+$40,600 (+406%)', could not be reconciled with anything else in the table until you guessed the account size. It reconciles exactly on a $10,000 test account at 2% risk: 156 trades x 1.3R x $200 = $40,560, and $40,600 on $10,000 is 406%. That is now stated in the row label, so the whole table is checkable rather than only most of it.
35-backtesting-reality.summary: This is the best lesson in the curriculum so far, and it is best precisely where the rest of the corpus has been weakest: it demolishes a fabricated performance record, in public, line by line, and shows its working. Chris's 'perfect' backtest is +1.3R expectancy, 4.9 profit factor, 67% win rate, +406% over two years. The lesson then accounts for every dollar of the gap between that and the -$8,400 he actually lost, in seven categories, and lands within $250 of the real figure. Every line of that accounting is checkable: 0.08% slippage on $25K over 37 round trips is $1,480; $0.65 per contract on 20 contracts over 37 round trips is $962; five missed winners at 1.8R less three avoided losers at 1.3R is -5.1R, which at $500 per R is $2,550. A reader who redoes the arithmetic finds it holds. The out-of-sample section then shows what would have caught it in advance, with the degradation figure (2023 expectancy 29% of 2022) doing the work. The first S grade in the intermediate tier. What earns it is not that the lesson is free of defects — it had five — but that its central artefact does the thing the rest of the curriculum needed doing to it: takes an impressive-looking performance record and shows, arithmetically, where the impression came from. The defects were at the edges: a dangling reference, upward-drifting thresholds, and three round numbers with nothing behind them. The seven-category cost autopsy in full, including every input, because every one of them can be recomputed. Chris's optimisation process (50 EMA periods x 20 ATR multipliers x 15 targets = 15,000 combinations), which is the mechanism of the failure. The in-sample/out-of-sample comparison and its 71% degradation. The walk-forward framework. The four ways backtests lie, each with a concrete example and a fix.
35-backtesting-reality.title: Backtesting Reality: That Perfect Expectancy Is Lying to You

fixes: Two genuine mathematical errors in the Risk of Ruin section, which is the section a reader is most likely to take on trust. A 50% win rate at 1:1 was given a Risk of Ruin of '~50%'; with no edge, gambler's ruin is certain — the correct figure is 100%, and it is a far better teaching point than the wrong one. And the practice exercise put Trader A's Risk of Ruin at '~40%' with the two traders '40x' apart; the formula the lesson itself supplies gives 13.4% and 0.004%, which is a factor of about 3,000. Both corrected. The exercise now asks the reader to compute the ratio rather than handing them a wrong one.

The RoR formula's exponent was labelled 'Max Trades' and glossed as 'max consecutive losses before ruin', which reads as the probability of a losing streak rather than the probability of ever going broke. It is units of capital — how many full-size losses fit in the account — and the lesson now says so, states the 1:1 payoff assumption the formula rests on, and draws out the two consequences: halving risk squares the survival odds, and at a 50% win rate the base becomes 1 and the whole expression collapses.

The composite's recovery record: '31 trades, 23 wins, max DD -8.4% vs -69.2% (-88% improvement) ... $15.4K → $27.7K (+79.9% recovery)'. The behavioural half survives — zero protocol violations in 26 weeks, worst week -$510 against -$9,200, worst drawdown 8.4% against 69.2% — because those describe what he did. The return does not. What replaces it is the arithmetic that actually justifies the whole lesson: recovering from a 69.2% drawdown requires a 225% gain.

Two counterfactuals. 'The math: reducing at -15% would have saved him $20K+' — not calculable, because the trades he took at full size are not the trades he would have taken at half size. And in his own quote, 'Those rules saved me from blowing the remaining $15K'. Both replaced; the quote now says the honest version, that he cannot know what he would have done without them. The checkable comparison stays: +17.6% to recover from -15%, +225% from -69.2%.

'Prop firms auto-liquidate at 8%', asserted three times as though it were a fact about portfolio heat. Funded-trading firms impose drawdown limits, not heat limits, and the thresholds vary widely between firms. Replaced with what is true and is the actual point: every such firm enforces some hard limit and closes you at it, and a limit you cannot override is worth more than a limit you intend to respect.
'This one check prevents 90% of account blowups' in the Quick Wins — an invented rate attached to an otherwise excellent two-minute instruction. The instruction stands on its own.
36-advanced-risk-management.summary: The three-tier structure is the right way to teach this: per-trade risk, portfolio heat, and drawdown, with the drawdown protocol explicitly overriding the other two. The first quiz question tests exactly that override — heat is fine at 7.5%, drawdown is -15%, and the answer is cut anyway — which is the one place traders reliably get it wrong. The Kelly section is unusually careful, and correct where most treatments are not: it derives full Kelly, refuses it, walks fractional Kelly down, and then makes the point that matters, which is that Kelly is a ceiling rather than a target and you take the lower of it and your per-trade cap. Kevin's disaster reconciles exactly ($34,600 is 69.2% of $50,000, leaving the $15.4K stated) and the escalation is the useful part: he averaged down fourteen times and increased size at -32%. This is the first lesson in the audit whose defects included real mathematical errors rather than only invented figures, and both were in the section with the most authority — a named formula with worked numbers. The formula itself was right; what was wrong was the label on its exponent and two of the three numbers plugged into it. Kevin's descent in full, week by week, including tripling down on BTC at -52%. The Kelly derivation and both worked examples, whose arithmetic checks out ((0.6x450 - 0.4x250)/450 = 0.378; (0.6x2 - 0.4)/2 = 0.40). The daily, pre-trade and post-trade checklists. The four practice scenarios. The cost-tracking quiz, which is the only place in the tier that makes a reader reconcile a broker statement against their own P&L and find a $200 gap.
36-advanced-risk-management.title: Advanced Risk Management: Professional Frameworks

fixes: A table of win rates and average R for Signal Pilot's own indicators — 'Janus only: 58% WR, 2.3R; Janus + Plutus: 66%, 3.1R; Janus + Plutus + Volume Oracle: 72%, 3.6R' — presented as what a reader's journal would show, and concluding 'Confluence dramatically improves edge'. This is the company publishing performance figures for its own products with nothing behind them, and it is the single worst instance found in the audit. Replaced with the same three-way split as a blank template, plus the reason the blanks are there, plus the trap the exercise walks into: requiring more confluence removes trades, so what is left looks better almost by construction. That is selection, not evidence, and the lesson now says so.

A second fabricated table, 'Performance by R:R', giving win rates by R:R bucket. Replaced with the same bucketing as a template and the observation that actually teaches: the win rate is supposed to fall as the target moves further away, so the column to read is total R, and a bucket can win 40% of the time and still be the best one.

Four extrapolations, each turning a small sample into an annual figure. '30 days x 1 trade/day = +$5,400/month ... a $60K/year leak' from twelve morning trades. 'Over 50 weeks, this saves $25K+' from three FOMO trades. 'Over 12 months = +$13,200 from ONE journal insight' from one month of 47 trades. 'This 10-minute exercise often reveals a $5K-10K annual leak' from five trades. All removed; the within-sample arithmetic that the reader can check is kept in every case.

'Week 2: 4 FOMO urges, skipped all 4, saved ~$1,300 in losses' — the counterfactual in its purest form, and the mirror image of the missed-profits fallacy this curriculum has been removing everywhere else. A skipped trade has no result. The lesson now says exactly that, names the symmetry with traders who credit themselves for profits they imagine they missed, and tells the reader to track compliance rather than savings.

Morgan's after-record, stated twice: 'monthly income went from $1,367 to $4,160 by closing the blind spot' and 'tripling it by trading LESS'. What replaces it is the change that can be reported honestly — Friday went from the most-traded day of the week to the least — and the observation that the intervention needed no strategy change, no new indicator, and no profit figure attached to be worth doing.

'If they'd simply skipped Fridays, their 6-month return would have been +16.9% instead of +8.2%' restated as what it actually is: Monday to Thursday, on their own, came to +16.9%. Same number, no counterfactual.
37-trade-journal-mastery.summary: The core argument is right and is made well: a journal is not a diary, it is a dataset, and its value comes entirely from segmenting it. Morgan's Friday leak is the best illustration of that idea in the corpus — the account was up 8.2% over six months, Monday to Thursday was up 16.9%, and the Friday losses came to 107% of everything the other four days had made. The reader can check that: 8,740 divided by 8,200 is 106.6%. And the cause the journal exposes is behavioural rather than market-related (51 trades on Fridays, the most of any day, forced to 'end the week green'), which is the whole point — the fix was a rule about one day of the week, not a new strategy. The Quick Wins are unusually well judged: six columns, thirty seconds a trade, a Sunday reminder. This lesson was teaching readers to be rigorous with their own data while modelling the opposite: two fabricated performance tables, four annualised extrapolations, one counterfactual saving, and one composite income record. The fix in every case was the same move the lesson already recommends elsewhere — report what the sample shows, and stop there. Morgan's full day-of-week breakdown, the 107% figure, and the behavioural root cause. Every piece of within-sample arithmetic in the three knowledge-check questions, all of which reconciles (12 x $180 = $2,160; 18 x -$95 = -$1,710; $4,200/20 = $210; -$1,100/15 = -$73; $1,680/12 = $140; $5,880 - $4,780 = $1,100 = +23%). The five-mistake taxonomy and the confluence scoring rubric.
37-trade-journal-mastery.title: Trade Journal Mastery: Systematic Improvement

fixes: Both composites carried recovery records. Rachel: '29 trades, 25 of them winners, 2.4:1 R:R, +$41K'. Michael: three week-blocks at +$3,200, +$4,800 and +$18,700, then 'Recovered $26,700 of the $47K loss, 23 winners in 28 trades against 14 in 43 before'. Removed in both cases, keeping the counts that describe behaviour rather than outcome: 29 trades where there had been 82, 28 where there had been 43, zero stop moves, zero revenge trades, 53 setups the checklist stopped her taking.

The $18K stop-discipline figure was stated as a saving three times ('NEVER moving stops saved $18K', 'she moved stops 0 times and saved approximately $18,000', and a quiz question built entirely on it). A saving from trades not taken is unknowable — but the same arithmetic run backwards is entirely sound, because those 34 stop moves DID happen and each one has a measurable cost. Reframed throughout as $17,850 incurred rather than $18,000 saved, and Q5 rewritten to ask what the habit cost and how you know, which turns a counterfactual question into a checkable one.
The same reframe applied to Michael: 'Stop discipline saved $16,200' became 'moving stops had cost him $16,200', which is nine moves x $1,800 and reconciles exactly.

'This 30-min ritual prevents 80% of bad trades', stated twice — an invented rate. Replaced with why the ritual works at all: it fixes your bias before the market gives you a reason to want a different one.

Three extrapolations. 'Over 50 weeks: -$600/week from rushed entries = -$30,000/year' from a single illustrative trade. And in the session-splitting question, an elaborate chain — '12 morning trades/15 days = 0.8/day x 20 days = 16 trades x $390 = +$6,240/month ... +$4,000/month (+$48K/year)' — built on twelve observed trades. Both replaced with what the sample does establish, which is that one session is paying for the other, and with the reason the forecast is not available: the mornings that produced those trades were the mornings that happened to offer setups.
'skip trade, saved $500 loss' in the Quick Wins — replaced with the observation that matters more than the imagined saving: three checklist items said no and you were about to click anyway.
'3-5 high-probability candidates daily' from the scanner output — the scanner filters on four stated criteria and cannot speak to probability. Now 'candidates that meet every criterion'.
38-professional-operations.summary: The claim this lesson makes is unusual for the genre and it is right: the thing separating two traders with identical strategies is often not the strategy at all. Both composites lose large sums while knowing exactly what a good setup looks like — Rachel woke at 9:45 for a 9:30 open and entered at daily resistance without ever checking it; Michael's backtests were profitable and he moved his stop nine times. The remedy is correspondingly unglamorous and specific: a 30-minute pre-market sequence with five named steps, a five-item entry checklist small enough to tape to a monitor, a 15-minute post-market review, and four circuit breakers. The single best thing in the lesson is a piece of arithmetic: moving a stop 34 times, each move turning a planned -$1,050 into a realised -$1,575, is $525 x 34 = $17,850 — a quarter of the whole disaster, from one habit, and the reader can verify every step of it. The pattern in this lesson is worth naming because it recurs across the tier: the same number is honest in one direction and fabricated in the other. What a bad habit cost is arithmetic on trades that happened. What a good rule saved is a guess about trades that did not. This lesson had the figure pointing the wrong way in five places; it now points the right way, and is stronger for it, because $17,850 of a $73,000 loss traceable to one repeated action is a more useful fact than a promise about the future. Both disasters in full, including every diagnostic detail: Rachel's 9:45 wake-up, 34 stop moves, 27 revenge trades and 26% win rate; Michael's 11-of-11 losses before 10:30, his eight no-confluence losses, and his nine stop moves. The complete pre-market, session and post-market phases with their timings. The workspace layouts, the automation tools, the four circuit breakers, and the weekly and monthly routines.
38-professional-operations.title: Professional Trading Operations: Workflow & Automation

fixes: The lesson defined the '@T' sale condition as 'Form T = late report = dark pool', repeated it in eleven places, built a Time & Sales filter instruction on it, and made it the subject of a quiz question. This is wrong. The T condition marks a trade executed outside regular market hours; it appears on pre-market and after-hours prints of every size and says nothing about whether a trade was internalised or crossed in an ATS. The identifier is the exchange code, 'D'. A reader following the old instruction would have filtered their tape down to extended-hours odd lots and concluded dark pools were full of 200-share trades. Corrected throughout, with the folklore named as folklore.

A second, contradictory error alongside it: 'delayed reporting: may appear 10 seconds to 30 minutes after actual execution', stated twice, while two other passages correctly said trades must be reported within 10 seconds. The 10-second rule is the true one; the half-hour delay is not a thing.

'40% of equity volume trades in dark pools', asserted four times — and then contradicted by the lesson's own Part 4, which correctly says most of that off-exchange share is wholesaler internalisation of retail orders, i.e. explicitly not dark pools. Rewritten to separate the two, because the distinction is the whole basis for calling one of them signal and the other noise.

'Citadel sees YOUR order before it's executed, can trade ahead (legal but controversial)' — trading ahead of a customer order is prohibited, and describing it as legal about a named firm is both wrong and unfair. Replaced with the argument people actually have about PFOF: whether a firm that sees most of the retail tape in aggregate gains an advantage from knowing its shape. The '$0.002/share' PFOF rate was also roughly an order of magnitude high for equities; corrected, with the note that options pay far more, which is the real reason brokers court that flow.

The 'Real Trade Example (September 2023)' was dated onto a calendar that refutes it: it places trades on September 3rd, a Sunday, and September 4th, Labor Day, and has SPY making new highs at $460 during a month in which SPY fell from about $451 to about $423. Converted to a numbered-day worked example, with the reason stated in the text.

Tyler's composite carried the same problem — 'October 15th' was a Sunday, and SPY was near $434 and falling on the October 12th the story needs at $459 — plus a quantified after-record ('Profit: $14,200 on 1,000 shares') and a testimonial. Dates removed, result removed, and the contrast that matters kept: the first short was taken because an indicator said the market had gone up a lot, the second because size was leaving while price went up.

Both trades quoted returns on margin at '10x leverage' — leverage not available on US equities to retail, where Reg T gives 2x overnight and 4x intraday. Replaced with R. The lesson now makes the point explicitly: dividing a fixed profit by a margin figure lets you print any percentage you like by choosing the denominator, which is why a return-on-margin claim should always prompt the question.
'Adds 5-8% to win rate' for the price/DIX divergence, and two 'high-probability' labels.
Added the correction the lesson was built without: the tape carries no side, so every 'buy print' in it is an inference. DIX now follows from that rather than floating free.

Replaced the DIX formula. It was written as Buy Volume / Total Dark Pool Volume, which describes a quantity nobody can observe; it is reconstructed from FINRA short-sale volume, and the bands no longer promise a rally in 1-5 days.

Killed the '40% of volume trades in dark pools' takeaway, which contradicted the lesson's own correction that dark pools are the smaller half of off-exchange volume and wholesaler internalisation is the larger.
Removed 'institutions front-ran retail' in both places. Front-running means trading ahead of a customer order you are handling; buying early is not it.
Rewrote Q4. 'No sellers left, only buyers' cannot happen -- every one of those prints had a seller in it -- and the +3-8% in 2-7 days was a schedule the mechanism does not support.
Gave the venue market-share table a denominator: shares of ATS volume, not of total US equity volume, republished weekly by FINRA.
strengths: The routing walkthrough -- why an institution wants the midpoint, and why 500,000 shares on a lit book would be front-run
Block-size thresholds scaled by instrument liquidity, which is a real piece of thinking
The @T correction, and now the unsigned-print correction beside it: both tell the reader to stop filtering on the wrong thing
Q5's absorption logic, correctly reasoned
39-dark-pool-indicators.summary: Re-read on its current state and raised from B. The earlier B was a penalty for what the lesson's errors had been rather than a description of the page, which is not a basis for a grade. Re-reading it turned up one genuine gap that mattered more than any of the original defects: the tape does not carry a side. A print has a time, a price, a size and a venue code, and nothing else -- every trade has a buyer and a seller in it, and nothing says which one went looking for the other. The lesson was built on 'dark pool buy prints' as though the side were readable, which is the same class of error as the @T folklore it already corrects. That correction now sits in Part 2 and makes DIX make sense for the first time: DIX exists precisely because the side is not readable, and is reconstructed from FINRA short-sale volume on the reasoning that a market maker filling a buyer has to short to do it. Four other things went with it: the Key Takeaway still said '40% of volume trades in dark pools', contradicting the lesson's own careful correction eight screens earlier; 'institutions front-ran retail' used a term that means trading ahead of a customer order you are handling, which is prohibited and has nothing to do with being early; Q4 answered 'no sellers left, only buyers', which cannot happen since every print had a seller in it, and attached a +3-8% move in 2-7 days to it; and the venue market-share table gave no denominator, so it now says the shares are of ATS volume rather than of total equity volume and that FINRA republishes them weekly. What was already strong is untouched: the routing walkthrough, the block-size thresholds scaled by instrument liquidity, the four print patterns, the complete long setup, and the absorption logic in Q5, which is the subtlest idea in the lesson and is correctly reasoned.
39-dark-pool-indicators.title: Dark Pool Indicators: Decoding Hidden Institutional Volume

fixes: The gamma sign was inverted. 'Positive GEX above price = dealers buy rallies (amplifies moves)' — it is the opposite. Long-gamma dealers sell into strength and buy into weakness, which compresses the range; the squeeze that ran Brandon over is a NEGATIVE gamma phenomenon. The lesson said this correctly elsewhere and contradicted itself here, in the framework paragraph, in the checklist, and in the Q5 explanation. A reader who learned the rule from the wrong passage would look for a squeeze in exactly the regime that suppresses one. Corrected in all three places, with the confusion named so the reader can spot it in other people's writing.

The missing caveat that makes 'never fight big flow' safe to hold. A large call print is not proof anybody is bullish: it can be one leg of a spread, an overwrite against stock already owned, a hedge on a short, or a dealer on the other side of all of them. The tape shows size and aggression, never the position the trade belongs to. Added before the recovery system, and made the subject of the rewritten Q4 — because the honest reading (hedging demand is certain, intent is invisible) is both more useful and more defensible than the version the lesson had.

Five invented hit rates: 'moves toward strike ~68% of time', 'P/C >1.5 precedes bounces ~72% within 1-5 days', 'moves toward max pain 64%', 'win rate OpEx days: ~60-65%', and '3-way confluence = 70-80% win rate'. Each removed and replaced with what is actually known — including, for pinning, that the academic work finds it far more clearly in single names with concentrated open interest than in an index ETF traded in SPY's size.

Brandon's composite after-record, in four places: the recovery line ('Gained $53K in 10 weeks, 51% recovery'), three constructed winning trades presented as the method working, the Results block, and — the worst of them — as the correct answer to Q4, which had to be rewritten around a real question. The before-record stays: 27 trades, 3 winners, -$96K is a disaster he lived, and it is the part that teaches.

Two absolutes: 'P/C extreme + structure hold = high-probability bottom' and 'this demonstrates why you NEVER fight massive institutional options flow'. The second replaced with the accurate version — big flow is not always right, it just creates hedging you have to trade against as well as the position itself.
Rewrote the learning objectives and the Real Talk box, which promised 'large call buying = bullish' and 'you're seeing institutional conviction' -- both of which Part 2 spends a paragraph refuting.
Fixed the case-study answer, which still ended '$5M+ call flow = go LONG'. That is the same mistake with the sign reversed.

Replaced the invented '$5M in, $50M+ out (10x)' payoff with the argument that survives checking: premium and exposure are different sizes, the premium is the entire floor, and the upside multiple depends on a path nobody can quote in advance.
Removed the ~70% and ~60% P/C hit rates, which contradicted this lesson's own quiz explanation that no reliable rate exists.

Corrected max pain. It is not the highest-OI strike; it is the settlement price that minimises what option sellers would have to pay out, and the two can differ when heavy put and call strikes sit far apart.

Removed 'dealers adjust hedges to push price toward max pain'. A delta-hedged dealer has no directional stake in settlement; what happens near a heavy strike is reactive long-gamma hedging, which is a drag rather than a destination.
De-dated the SPY UOA worked example, whose calendar did not survive checking against what SPY did that week, and said so on the page.
Fixed the closing exercise, which asked the reader to compare win rates over ten trades against ten trades.
strengths: The premise is unusually well chosen: options matter to an equity trader because of the hedging they force, not because of what the buyer believes
The UOA screen -- volume against open interest, premium size, execution aggression -- is concrete and reproducible
The directional-bet versus hedging table, which is the distinction most flow commentary skips
Brandon's blowup: he was short into $35M of call flow and the dealers hedging it, and had accounted for neither
40-options-order-flow.summary: Re-read on its current state and raised from B. The earlier B was a penalty for what the lesson's errors had been, which is not a basis for grading the page. Re-reading turned up a sharper problem: the lesson contradicted its own central caveat, and did so in the first thing a reader sees. Part 2 says plainly that a large call print is not proof anyone is bullish -- it may be one leg of a spread, an overwrite against stock already held, or a hedge on a short -- and that the useful reading is 'someone has an exposure and dealers must hedge it'. But the learning objectives still opened with 'Large call buying = bullish', the Real Talk box still said 'when you see this flow, you're seeing institutional conviction', and the case-study answer still ended '$5M+ call flow = go LONG'. A reader who took the objectives at face value learned the opposite of the lesson. All three now agree with Part 2. Four more went with them: the 'spend $5M, make $50M+ (10x return)' payoff was invented and has been replaced by the argument that actually holds, which is that premium and exposure are different sizes and the premium is the whole floor; the ~70% and ~60% P/C hit rates were still standing three screens from a quiz explanation saying nobody has a reliable one; max pain was defined as the highest-OI strike, which is not what it is; and the body still had dealers pushing price toward it, which a delta-hedged dealer has no reason to do. What was already strong is untouched: the UOA screen and its three filters, the GEX and zero-gamma material, the pinning caveat, the confluence worked example with its R arithmetic, and Brandon's blowup, which remains the best disaster record in the tier.
40-options-order-flow.title: Options Order Flow: Following Smart Money Gamma

fixes: 'YOUR profit is someone else's loss. That makes trading a zero-sum game' — the lesson's opening premise, and false as stated. Equities as a whole are not zero-sum; futures are zero-sum before costs and negative-sum after. What is close to zero-sum is short-horizon trading against other short-horizon traders, which is exactly what the lesson is about, so the argument survives intact once stated precisely.

The manipulation story, which ran through the whole lesson: institutions 'sweep stops' as a deliberate 'dominant strategy'. Deliberately pressing price to trigger stops rather than to trade at those prices is manipulation and is prosecuted. The observable phenomenon needs no such story: stops cluster below the obvious level because that is where every course puts them, and a buyer who needs size wants to be filled where supply is. Same conclusion, no conspiracy, and a reader who learns the second version will not spend their career looking for villains. The actionable advice is unchanged.

'Institutions can coordinate legally (through prime brokerage relationships, shared research, dark pool order flow visibility)' with a supporting list — prime brokers sharing client order-flow patterns is what information barriers exist to prevent, and dark pools are dark by construction: you cannot see other participants' resting orders in one. Also 'retail traders can't coordinate (illegal to collude)' — agreeing where to put stops would not be illegal, it is merely impossible to arrange. Replaced with how a large participant actually infers where liquidity sits, which needs no coordination at all and makes the coordination-failure point better.

Part 2 was titled 'Prisoner's Dilemma in Liquidity Provision' and then presented a stop-placement decision matrix that is not a prisoner's dilemma — there is no cooperative option for you and a large buyer to abandon. Named plainly, in a lesson about game theory, and pointed at the place where the structure genuinely does appear.

Q2's answer had market makers 'committing to provide liquidity regardless'. They widen and step back when adverse selection rises, which is exactly why spreads blow out in a panic; they are paid to carry the risk, not sworn to ignore it. Rewritten, including what a designated market maker's quoting obligation actually guarantees.

Eight invented figures: '60-70% vs 40-45%' win rates for the two strategies, '60-70% of reversals have sweeps' (twice), '80% place stops just below support' (twice), 'win rate jumps to 70%+', 'you survive 70% more sweeps', and a 30% failure rate the exercise never supplied. The 65% in the expected-value calculation was kept as a stated assumption, with the arithmetic run at 50%, 40% and the 37.5% break-even so the reader can see how fast the edge dies.

'Real Example: ES Futures Support Sweep (June 2024)' — constructed minute by minute, and ES was nowhere near 5250 that June. Converted to an undated worked example, with the unobservable '10,000+ retail longs with stops at 5245-5248' replaced by what a chart actually shows, and two headline totals ($9M-11.5M, $12.5M) removed: the contract count they multiply is not observable.

Sarah's after-record ('18 trades, 13 winners, $14,150 in 2 months') and her testimonial. Her three months of false stop-outs stay — 23 stops at $750 is arithmetic on trades that happened, and it is the part that teaches.

Rewrote Strategy #2. It had institutions deliberately randomising when they hunt stops to stop retail adapting -- a single coordinating actor with a schedule, which is precisely what Part 1 spends a page showing is unnecessary. The randomness is structural: uncoordinated firms on different clocks with different sizes to fill.
Rewrote Q4 and its takeaway to match, and made the point that the distinction changes the advice: there is no schedule to learn, so the answer is construction rather than prediction.
Fixed the learning objectives, which still promised 'Where are stops clustered? Institutions will sweep them' and 'expect opposite institutional move'.
Fixed Condition 2 of the dominant-action argument, which required a reversal probability above 50% while the EV arithmetic three lines below puts breakeven at about 37.5%.
Removed the invented 70/30 sweep frequency, and rebuilt Exercise 2 on a scenario that deliberately withholds the split -- because live trading withholds it too.
Corrected Exercise 2's answer. A split entry does not mean 'you always catch the move': if the level holds you are filled on half your size at the level, and that is the trade a split actually makes.
Flagged the 15,000 stops in Exercise 1 as a premise of the exercise rather than something observable, since Part 1 says stops are not in the book until they trigger.
strengths: The central idea is rare in trading education and correct: your stop is a move in a game where the other side knows what traders like you typically do
The three levels of reasoning are the Keynesian beauty contest applied properly
The Level 3 stop framework -- thesis invalidation plus a volatility buffer -- is the most actionable idea in the tier, and every piece of its arithmetic checks out
The payoff matrix is labelled as illustrative ranks rather than measured payoffs, and the dominance argument in it is valid
41-game-theory-trading.summary: Re-read on its current state and raised from B. The old B was history: it graded the lesson on what its errors had been. Re-reading found something worse and more interesting -- Part 3 reinstated the exact conspiracy Part 1 spends a page dismantling. Part 1 says plainly that nobody has to hunt anybody: stops cluster below an obvious level because that is where every course puts them, a buyer with size wants to be filled where the supply is, and the two facts together explain the tape with no coordination at all. Then Strategy #2 said institutions 'use mixed strategies (randomize sweep timing)' to 'prevent retail adaptation' -- which needs a single coordinating actor setting a schedule, the one thing Part 1 had just argued you do not need. The fix keeps the game theory and drops the cartel: the randomness is real and comes from structure, not intent -- different firms, different mandates, different sizes to fill, different clocks, no channel between them. That is a mixed strategy nobody chose, and Part 1's own note that Nash equilibria may exist only in mixed strategies now pays off instead of sitting unused. It also changes the advice: if a coordinator set the schedule you would try to learn the schedule; since none exists, the response is construction rather than prediction, which is what the Level 3 stop framework was already telling you. Four more: the objectives still promised 'Institutions will sweep them'; Condition 2 required a reversal probability above 50% while the lesson's own EV arithmetic puts breakeven at 37.5%; the invented 70/30 sweep frequency was still there and Exercise 2 was built on it; and Exercise 2's answer claimed a split entry means 'you always catch the move', which is false -- if the level holds you get half the size, and that is the actual trade a split makes.
41-game-theory-trading.title: Game Theory in Trading: Adversarial Thinking

fixes: The forced-unwind myth, throughout. A dealer short calls that finish in the money does not sell the hedge — the calls are exercised and the hedge is DELIVERED. Calls that finish out of the money see their hedge run off as delta decays, which follows the move rather than causing it. And the flow is not one-directional: a dealer short puts that expire worthless has to buy back short stock at the same moment. Replaced with what actually happens, plus the reason it matters: 'buy puts at 3 PM on OpEx Friday' requires knowing which way price leaves the strike before the flow tells you anything, which is the whole problem.

A direct internal contradiction. Part 1 says dealers short options amplify moves (buy higher, sell lower); Part 3's charm section runs that exact mechanic and concludes 'price pins to the strike'. Those are opposite outcomes. Pinning requires dealers to be LONG gamma at the strike; short gamma pushes price away. Both signs now stated, with the research finding noted: expiration clustering shows up where market makers are net long the strike and anti-clustering where they are net short.

The definition of max pain — 'the strike where the most options expire worthless, maximum profit for market makers' — is wrong twice. It is the strike minimising total intrinsic payout (a different number, since cheap and expensive contracts do not weigh the same), and market makers are hedged and roughly flat, not the net writers. Corrected, and the section headed 'How to Calculate Max Pain', which had a heading and no body at all, now has the five-step calculation with a worked fragment and a statement of the two things it cannot tell you.

The vanna table gave one sign for 'calls' when vanna changes sign across the strike, and concluded that falling IV is bearish. In index books, where customers are net buyers of downside puts, falling IV releases dealers from short stock hedges — this is the vanna tailwind that lifts markets after an event passes. The lesson's trade instruction, 'short SPY when VIX drops below 20', was therefore backwards on a well-documented relationship. Removed with the reasoning shown.

The Volmageddon timeline: the jobs report was Friday 2 February, not 1 PM on Monday the 5th; the VIX move (17.31 to 37.32, about +116%) was a full day, not 2.5 hours; VIX above 50 was the following morning; XIV's indicative value fell about 96%, not 100%. Also 'VIX spikes to 30-60 two or three times per year' — in most calendar years since 1990 it does not happen at all.

The opening paragraph, which multiplied 200,000 contracts by full notional to get a $9 billion hedge (at 0.50 delta it is about $4.5 billion) and assumed dealers were short all of them. That assumption — open interest equals dealer short position — ran silently through every figure in the lesson and is now stated wherever it is used.

'Citadel is now delta-neutral (profit from theta decay)' — a delta-hedged short call earns theta and pays gamma, and only makes money if realised volatility comes in under implied. The half that can bankrupt you was missing.

The put/call row in the dealer-positioning table gave the identical reading — 'dealers short gamma' — for both a high and a low ratio, which cannot be a signal. GME's dealer hedge figures ('150M+ shares, 3x the float') were invented and impossible, exceeding shares outstanding; removed rather than guessed at. Tool subscription prices removed, with the point that every gamma service is running a model, not reporting data.

Both composites' after-records: Kyle's recovery trade and 12-trade, 75% record; Sarah's TSLA trade, +$60K, and 14-trade, 78.6%, +$184.3K record; both testimonials; and the trailing recovery line on Sarah's quiz card. The disasters stay — $67,200 in 45 minutes and $96,000 in six hours are what the lesson is for.

The playbook: two invented win rates (65% monthly, 68% zero-day), four constructed winning example trades, and the recommendation to sell a naked at-the-money straddle on expiration day. That last one is the most dangerous instruction in the audited curriculum so far: undefined maximum loss, assignment risk in exactly the scenario the trade is built on, and a high win rate offered as the reason to take it.

Fixed 'Trading Gamma Squeezes', which told the reader to exit before expiration because dealers will dump hedges -- the forced unwind this lesson has a boxed section demolishing. The exit is now when fresh call buying slows, which is the actual fuel and is observable.

Corrected the GME collapse, attributed to dealers unwinding at expiration. Several brokers restricted opening buy orders on 28 January, the inflow stopped, and a price held up by continuous buying could not stay there without it.

Rewrote the three steps in 'Trading Vanna Squeeze', which asserted a mechanism the paragraph immediately below called backwards. Falling IV shrinks the short-put delta that dominates an index dealer book, so dealers buy stock back -- a tailwind, not a drag.

Fixed the vanna 'why it matters' line, which taught the simple version that the table directly beneath it refutes. Vanna changes sign across the strike, and an index book is made of short puts rather than calls.

Removed the entry from the post-earnings vanna box. The unwind exhausting tells you the next move is opinion rather than hedging; it does not tell you which way, and the note underneath already said so.

Replaced the VIX row in the dealer-positioning table, which read the gamma sign off VIX. Dealers being short gamma is one of the causes of the volatility VIX measures, so that is inferring the cause from the effect -- and it agrees with GEX precisely except when you would want it to disagree.
strengths: The delta-hedging walkthrough, including the correction that a hedged short call earns theta and pays gamma rather than simply 'collecting decay'
Max pain computed properly by hand, with the two things the calculation cannot tell you stated plainly
The boxed 'forced 4 PM unwind is not a thing' correction, which is the lesson's best single page
The Volmageddon reconstruction, with the jobs report on the right Friday and the XIV decline stated as measured rather than rounded to a total loss
42-options-market-microstructure.summary: Re-read on its current state and raised from C. The C was earned at the time: the lesson's spine was the claim that dealers are obliged to liquidate into the close on expiration Friday, and that claim is false. The prose was rewritten around the honest explanation -- Kyle and Sarah bought same-day options and needed a specific move within hours, which is a complete account needing no villain. What re-reading found is that the correction stopped at the prose. Every actionable box still carried the old mechanism, and a box is what a reader acts on. 'Trading Gamma Squeezes' told you to exit before expiration because dealers will dump their hedges -- the forced unwind the lesson devotes a boxed warning to demolishing eight screens earlier -- and the GME collapse from $483 was attributed to the same thing rather than to the brokers who restricted opening buy orders on 28 January and the inflow that stopped with them. 'Trading Vanna Squeeze' listed three steps that are backwards, then a paragraph underneath saying they are backwards; the steps now say what actually happens, which is that falling IV shrinks the short-put delta dominating an index book and dealers buy stock back. The vanna 'why it matters' line taught the everywhere-repeated version the table directly below it refutes. The post-earnings box gave an entry the note under it retracts. And the dealer-positioning table read the gamma sign off VIX, which is reading the cause off the effect: dealers being short gamma is one of the things that makes VIX high. What was always strong is untouched -- the delta-hedging walkthrough with its theta-versus-gamma correction, the max-pain arithmetic worked by hand, the charm mechanics, and the Volmageddon reconstruction with its dates fixed.
42-options-market-microstructure.title: Options Market Microstructure: How Dealers Move Markets

fixes: 'A 2020 SEC study found... $1.5 billion/year.' No such study. Removed and replaced with what the evidence actually shows: academic work sending identical orders through multiple brokers simultaneously found large, persistent differences in the prices that came back, while brokers' own Rule 605 execution-quality reports show most marketable retail orders receiving some price improvement. Both are true, and the real argument is about the size of the improvement rather than about being filled outside the quote.

Spoofing, layering and quote stuffing were attributed to market makers as routine practice — 'MM posts fake sell order', 'market maker manipulation', 'illegal-but-common'. The enforcement record is overwhelmingly against proprietary traders, individuals and bank desks, not the registered wholesalers that fill retail orders. Reattributed throughout, with what the prosecutions have actually been.

The spoofing detection rule: 'orders 5-10x larger than surrounding levels that vanish within 60 seconds = 80% likely spoofing; track ten and if eight vanish you have confirmed it.' This is wrong in a way that matters. The great majority of orders in US equities are cancelled rather than executed and have been for over a decade — eight of ten vanishing is what you see in a market with no spoofing in it at all. Replaced with the usable version: do not lean on a large resting order, whatever the intent behind it.

The PFOF quiz scenario, which does not hold together: it posits a seller resting at $100.01 on NYSE while the fill happens at $100.02. If that were so, $100.01 would BE the national best offer and the fill would be a trade-through — a violation, not a loophole. Rewritten around the real complaint, which is that no one else got to compete for the right to fill the order.

'Citadel receives your order 2 milliseconds before public exchanges... Why it's legal.' Trading ahead of a customer order is prohibited. The same class of error as the Citadel claim corrected in lesson 36.

'Market sell orders are ALWAYS filled at the bid.' Marketable retail orders frequently receive price improvement between the quotes — it is the main thing wholesalers sell to brokers — and an order larger than the displayed size walks the book and does worse.

The PFOF rate of $0.002/share for equities, roughly ten times too high, and every dollar figure built on it (Robinhood's $36M, Citadel's $180M, the $144M net). Removed rather than recalculated: the per-share rate is not published in a form you can multiply, and the argument does not need a total.

Two internal contradictions: 'trade illiquid times, pre-market has less HFT activity' directly against Strategy #2's 'avoid after-hours, spreads are 15x wider'; and AAPL's opening spread quoted as 5x wider in one place and 8x in another, same stock, same morning.

The IEX speed bump described as preventing front-running of retail orders — it protects orders RESTING on IEX from stale-quote pickoff, and does nothing for a marketable order sent there. The blanket 'Fidelity, Vanguard, Interactive Brokers don't take PFOF' list, wrong in the details about all three. The $300 million attributed to microwave towers, which actually belongs to the fibre line the microwaves made obsolete. Sarao presented as the cause of the Flash Crash, which the official joint report attributed to a large sell algorithm.

Eric's prior-year winning record (+$87K on 2,400 trades) and his recovery record ($72K to $110K, 52% to 67%), repeated four times. The $68,000 loss stays, and so does the arithmetic that produced it. The cost model was also corrected: most of the $0.10 a share was the spread, which a market order pays by definition and which was wide because of WHEN he traded — a dime a share is not reachable in SPY at 11 AM, and saying so makes the lesson narrower and more useful.

Rewrote the learning objectives, which promised 'Watch for MM inventory signals, aggressive quote lowering = distribution, fade rallies'. Inventory is not observable, the Key Takeaways say so explicitly, and fade-rallies appears nowhere else in the lesson.
Fixed the hook, which said market makers 'profit from EVERY transaction'. Part 2 is entirely about the orders that cost them money, and that is why the spread exists.
Changed 'inventory manipulation' to inventory management in the opening summary, matching Part 3's own title and content -- hedging and quote skewing, not anything improper.
Reframed the quote-stuffing objective, which presented a prosecutable practice as routine market-maker behaviour the reader should learn to spot.
strengths: Eric's arithmetic: execution cost compounds with frequency, and the sum kills the edge before any trade thesis is tested
The Dark Side section, which names who the enforcement record is actually against instead of implying wholesalers
The correction to the spread-capture arithmetic: a full penny on every share exceeds the firm's reported revenue across all asset classes
The PFOF section, which separates what the evidence supports from what is asserted about it
43-market-maker-algorithms.summary: Re-read on its current state and raised from C. The C was for the evidence: a citation to a regulator study that does not exist, repeated accusations of criminal conduct against named firms, and a spoofing-detection rule that would have a reader seeing manipulation in the ordinary behaviour of every order book in the country. All of that was fixed, and the Dark Side section is now one of the better pages in the tier -- it says plainly that the enforcement record for spoofing and layering is against proprietary traders and bank desks rather than the wholesalers filling retail orders, and the Key Takeaways add that you cannot identify either from a Level 2 screen because most orders are cancelled rather than filled. What re-reading found is that the opening had not been brought along with the body. The objectives still promised a framework the lesson never teaches and its own takeaways deny: 'Watch for MM inventory signals, aggressive quote lowering = distribution, fade rallies'. A market maker's inventory is not observable, the lesson says so five screens later, and 'fade rallies' appears nowhere else on the page -- the actual defence taught here is limit orders, liquid hours and knowing how your broker routes. The hook said dealers 'profit from EVERY transaction', which Part 2 exists to contradict: adverse selection is the informed flow that costs them money, and it is why spreads exist at all. And the opening summary listed 'inventory manipulation' where Part 3 is titled Inventory Management and describes hedging and quote skewing. That last one is small but it is the lesson's own diagnosed failure mode: a loaded word doing work the arithmetic was already doing better. Eric's case study is untouched and remains the best thing here -- $0.10 a share, 300 shares, 60 trades a day, and the edge is gone before you have been wrong about anything.
43-market-maker-algorithms.title: Market Maker Algorithms: How They Profit From You

fixes: The central claim — 'QE = liquidity expanding = bullish, QT = liquidity contracting = bearish' — is refuted by 2023 and 2024, in both of which the Fed ran quantitative tightening all year and the S&P gained roughly 24% and then 23%. The lesson asserted the rule in six places and never mentioned the two years that break it. Corrected throughout, and the correction strengthens the lesson rather than weakening it: the RRP drained roughly $2T over the same period, offsetting the balance-sheet runoff, which is precisely why Part 2's three-term net-liquidity measure exists. The balance sheet is now presented as one term of three rather than as the answer.

The Quick Wins list told the reader to check WALCL every Sunday and read a falling line as bearish — the exact instruction the 2023-24 record refutes. Rewritten to send the reader to Part 2 before acting on a falling balance sheet.

A run of invented hit rates and percentages attached to macro claims, none of which anyone has measured over a sample that exists: two QE cycles and two QT cycles is four observations, and the lesson was quoting rates off them.

The two-hour rule's positive form — 'holds into the close, buy tomorrow; fades into the close, short tomorrow' — is a coin flip dressed as a rule, with no evidence offered anywhere in the lesson. Kept the negative form, which is genuinely useful: stay out of the window where spreads are widest and the first move is most often wrong. The 'spreads widen 3-5x' multiple was replaced with the instruction to measure it once on your own instrument.

Absolutist position-sizing prescriptions — specific percentage portfolios per regime, presented as what to hold rather than as illustrations — plus 'every pullback is a gift', which is the sentence that gets a reader fully invested into the pullback that is not.
Rewrote the learning objectives, which contradicted each other in a single list: the first says 'QT = bearish' failed in 2023, the third and fourth then asserted exactly that rule.

Replaced the 'Fed funds rate changes lag' fragment with what it was presumably meant to say -- the policy rate moves in steps, months apart, after the data, so it tells you where the Fed has been while net liquidity tells you what is happening to reserves now.

Removed 'retail traders who ignored Fed policy lost everything, institutions who tracked net liquidity went short and profited'. Nobody has measured the first, and hedge funds as a group had a poor 2022 too.

Fixed the opening instruction of the Quick Wins box, which still told the reader to label a rising line bullish and a falling line bearish -- the exact step Part 2 argues against and the rest of that same box then documents.
Made the QT portfolio's leverage rule match the QE portfolio's, which had already been corrected to decide leverage from what a 20% adverse move does to the account rather than from the regime label.
strengths: The net-liquidity formula, with each term explained by its effect on reserves and every FRED series named
The Fed Put section, which says the strike moves, that it is not a promise, and that 2022 is the counter-example
The FOMC discipline: size down or sit out, no market orders in the first minutes, the announcement is not a trade
The 2022 figures now distinguish calendar-year from peak-to-trough instead of mixing them
44-fed-policy-liquidity.summary: Re-read on its current state and raised from B. The net-liquidity construction at the centre -- Fed balance sheet minus the Treasury General Account minus the reverse repo facility, each term explained by what it physically does to bank reserves, with the FRED series named so a reader can plot it -- is the best macro machinery in the curriculum, and the Fed Put section was already careful before any of this. The B was for the headline thesis, which 2023 and 2024 contradict, and the corrections had reached the body: the Quick Reference now says to read Part 2 before acting on a falling balance sheet, and the Quick Wins entry lays out two episodes that agree and two that disagree. What re-reading found is that the learning objectives had not been brought along, and they contradicted each other inside a single bullet list. The first objective says 'QT = bearish' failed in 2023. The third says 'Expanding = risk-on, contracting = risk-off'. The fourth says 'Monitor Fed balance sheet, contracting = reduce size'. All three now say the same thing, which is the thing the lesson actually teaches: read net liquidity, not the headline, and treat a falling balance sheet as a question. Two more: the Harsh Reality claimed retail 'lost everything' and that institutions 'went short and profited', neither of which anyone has measured and the second of which is false for hedge funds as a group in 2022; and the QT portfolio's leverage rule kept the reasoning that the QE portfolio directly above it corrects.
44-fed-policy-liquidity.title: Fed Policy & Liquidity Cycles: The Macro Trading Edge

strengths: Explains the most common complaint in retail options trading -- right on direction, lost money -- as the contract working exactly as priced rather than as bad luck.
Keeps the two forces separate: the move must exceed what was priced, and the event premium collapses regardless of direction once the news is out.
Refuses to endorse either side. Selling event premium wins most of the time and pays for it occasionally, which is a payoff shape rather than an edge.
The counter-intuitive close is earned: the events you can prepare for are the ones where preparation is worth least, because everyone else prepared too and it is in the price.
45-trading-scheduled-events.summary: New lesson on the events that carry a date, which had four single mentions across the curriculum. The artefact is the implied move read straight off the option chain -- straddle divided by price -- which converts 'earnings are risky' into a specific bar the event has to clear. A $6 straddle on a $100 stock means a 4% move on a correct directional call still loses, and the chain said so in advance.
45-trading-scheduled-events.title: Trading Around Scheduled Events

fixes: The SKEW index moves the opposite way from the direction this lesson assumed. Because it measures the out-of-the-money tail relative to at-the-money, SKEW typically FALLS in a panic — at-the-money implied volatility rises faster than the tail — and it runs high in calm markets. It fell during the COVID crash; its record above 170 came in June 2021 with the S&P at an all-time high and VIX in the mid-teens. The lesson had 'SKEW >155 = extreme fear, crash fears overdone → sell OTM puts', a worked example claiming SKEW 'spiked to 157' during the March 2023 banking crisis (it went down), and a quiz answer built on the same premise. Corrected in five places. The March 2023 trade survives on its own merits, because it never actually depended on the index reading — only on the ten-point gap between two implied volatilities you can see on any option chain.

The flagship long-volatility example claimed VIX April $20 calls went from $0.85 to $18.50 during Volmageddon — a 21-bagger — because spot VIX more than doubled. VIX options settle against the VIX FUTURE for their expiration month, not against spot. The April future went from the middle teens to the low twenties; that call was worth a few dollars. The enormous multiples that week were in February and March. This is arguably the most important single fact in VIX trading and the lesson had it exactly backwards in its own worked example, so the correction is now stated as a mechanical fact in Part 1 and demonstrated where the error was.

The 'VIX Mean Reversion Statistics (2000-2024)' table quoted a frequency for each band and a 'percent lower 30 days later' figure running from 92% to 18%. Those were not measured, and the methodology they imply is the error the case study is about: VIX above 40 is not thousands of independent trials since 2000, it is four or five episodes each contributing dozens of overlapping daily observations that all resolve together. Columns removed, direction kept, reasoning stated.

The October 2023 example ran its price path backwards. VIX did not spike from 13.6 to 22 on the October 7 attack; it was already near 17 and closed lower on the 9th while equities rallied, reaching roughly 21.7 on October 20 before falling to about 15 by November 3. Rewritten from the actual sequence — which is a better lesson, because the trade taken on the date the old version recommended spends ten days losing and gets stopped out by the lesson's own stop rule before being proved right.

The case study's contract counts were off by a factor of ten throughout: '15x VIX $15/$18 call spreads, max risk $45K' is $4,500 of risk, not $45,000. Corrected to 150/100/80 spreads, which makes every dollar figure in the story consistent — and reveals the real point: at about $0.35 credit on a $3-wide spread, the position's entire upside was roughly $11,000 against $99,000 of risk. She was risking nine dollars to make one, visible on the screen before the first trade. The reported mark of '+$16,800 (98% max profit)' was impossible, since max profit on a short spread is the credit collected; corrected to about $8,600.

'Kelly Criterion' was used to label what is actually an expectancy calculation. Both are now named correctly, and the conclusion sharpened: a negative expectancy makes the Kelly size negative, which is not 'size down' — it means the correct position was the other side of the trade or none at all.

SVXY was described as 'the inverse of VXX' with '+5 to +15% per month' and 2017's +185% quoted as its track record. SVXY has been a -0.5x product since February 2018; the instrument that returned 185% no longer trades. UVXY was described as 2x; it has been 1.5x since the same date. Both corrected, along with the symmetric decay claim — a daily-rebalanced inverse does not earn the decay of what it inverts.

'Net debit: $15 (this is your max risk)' on a position that is short an SPX straddle. It is not. Corrected, along with the note that the sketch's legs are mismatched by orders of magnitude because a real dispersion book is vega-weighted.

A Quick Win told the reader that buying SVXY when VIX hit 60-80 in March 2020 'profited massively'. Anyone who did that in the second week of March watched it fall for another week first. The framework table's 'sell VIX calls' also contradicted the lesson's own risk warning against naked VIX calls, in three places.

Corrected the realized-versus-implied objective, which was backwards. You are paid implied and pay out realized, so options are expensive when implied is above realized; the old line told the reader to sell in exactly the conditions where selling loses money.

Fixed the framework objective, which paired VIX above 30 with contango and VIX below 15 with backwardation -- inverted on both counts -- and recommended naked short VIX calls, four screens from the section explaining that uncapped short volatility is how accounts end.
Rewrote the mean-reversion objective, which said 'VIX >30 = sell volatility'. That is the trade this lesson's case study exists to describe.
Fixed the matching Key Takeaway, which still carried '(>30 = sell, <12 = buy)' as an instruction.
strengths: The VIX-to-expected-range table, which is arithmetically correct and the most useful thing on the page
The case study: 84% of trades won and the account destroyed anyway, because probability is not magnitude
The contango/backwardation explanation and the roll-decay example, accurately described
The Volmageddon material, with the short-volatility-has-no-maximum-loss point made where it belongs
46-volatility-trading-strategies.summary: Re-read on its current state and raised from C. The C was for four factual inversions in the body, and those were fixed: the SKEW index reads as the price of the tail rather than a crash alarm, the 2017 SVXY figures are marked as describing an instrument that no longer trades, the divide-by-16 conversion was added, and the case study -- a trader who won 84% of her trades and was destroyed anyway, because probability is not magnitude -- is the most valuable disaster in the curriculum. What re-reading found is that all four learning objectives were still the pre-correction ones, and two of them are factually wrong rather than merely stale. 'If realized > implied, sell options (overpriced)' is backwards: you are paid implied and you pay out realized, so options are expensive when implied is above realized -- the line told the reader to sell into exactly the conditions that make selling lose. The framework bullet paired VIX above 30 with contango and VIX below 15 with backwardation, which is inverted on both counts, since a panic puts the curve into backwardation and a calm market into contango; and it recommended selling naked VIX calls, which have no maximum loss, four screens from a section explaining that a short volatility position without a long option is how accounts end. The first objective told the reader to sell volatility at VIX 30, which is the trade the case study is about. And the Key Takeaway carried the same '>30 = sell' instruction. The objectives now describe what the lesson teaches: convert the level to an expected range, size from the range, and never carry short volatility uncapped.
46-volatility-trading-strategies.title: Volatility Trading Strategies: VIX, Skew & Dispersion

fixes: The central correction. 'Stocks vs Bonds (Inverse Correlation -0.3 to -0.7)' was presented as structural. The sign of that correlation depends on which shock dominates: growth shocks give the inverse relationship everyone knows, inflation and rates shocks flip it positive, and 2022 was the clearest positive-correlation year in decades — the S&P and long Treasuries both fell, which is why 60/40 had its worst year in a century. Rewritten as a conditional, which makes the rest of the lesson cohere: the autumn 2023 case study is a rates-shock episode, so TLT falling alongside SPY was the mechanism, not a divergence from it.

The rule that followed from the error: 'SPY + TLT both down >1% same day → exit ALL risk positions, go to cash, wait for correlations to normalize (usually 1-4 weeks).' Applied to 2022 that instruction leaves you in cash for two years waiting for a normalisation that is not coming, because nothing is broken. Replaced with the test that actually distinguishes a liquidation from a rates repricing: in a liquidation the dollar and cash are the only things bid and the selling is indiscriminate; in a repricing the selling is orderly, credit behaves, gold often holds.

'January 2020: SPY at all-time highs, HYG lagging, credit spreads widening. 2 months later: COVID crash. Credit warned first.' It did not. High-yield spreads were near cycle tights in January 2020 and HYG turned within a day of SPY in late February. This mattered because it was the flagship example for the signal the lesson calls most reliable. Replaced with a warning about hindsight-fitting the divergence.

The copper lead time. 'Copper moves 2-4 weeks BEFORE stocks' was contradicted by the lesson's own example: copper peaked on 20 May 2024, SPY not until 16 July — a two-month lead, during which selling on the copper signal would have cost an 8% rally. The example was also mis-dated to July. Corrected in four places, with the honest characterisation: usually early, sometimes very early, occasionally wrong, and therefore a reason to stop adding rather than a reason to go flat.

The composite's after-record: '18 trades, 14 winners, +$21K, $91K → $112K (+23%)' over Nov 2023 - Feb 2024. That window was one of the strongest four-month equity runs in years; almost any long held through it made money, so the figure measures the rally rather than the checklist. Removed, and replaced with what the checklist actually said on the relevant dates, which is checkable.

'When yields rise this fast, stocks MUST fall', twice, plus '+85 bps in 8 weeks — historic move', also twice. 2013 and 2021 are both counter-examples to the first and 2022 produced several larger moves than the second.

'About 40% of S&P 500 revenue comes from overseas' — the figure has been closer to 30% for some years. 'Q1 2022: SPY dropped from $480 to $410 over the same quarter' — that took until mid-May, which matters because it makes the dollar signal early rather than coincident. 'When 10Y yield spikes +10 bps, SPY typically drops 0.5-1.0%' and 'saves 50% of confusion', both invented.
'Real Trade Examples / Live Trades' relabelled as worked reconstructions, with the note that they cannot show you the occasions when the same signals lined up and the market went the other way.
Rewrote the learning objectives, which still printed Bonds/Stocks -0.5 as a constant, called 'stocks up and bonds up' unusual, and quoted a copper lead time the published work does not agree on.

Fixed the Key Takeaway that said stocks and bonds falling together is systemic risk and an immediate exit signal. It described 2022 and the autumn of 2023 too -- the period this lesson's own case study covers -- and those were inflation-and-rates regimes. The reading is 'my hedge is not hedging'.
Fixed 'when all assets move together, go to cash', which is an argument for smaller size; a reader who went to cash on it in early 2022 and waited for correlations to normalise sat out two years.

Removed 'DXY above 105 = bearish for SPY' as a trading signal. DXY was above 105 for long stretches of 2023 and 2024 while the S&P made new highs; the mechanism is sound but the level is not the signal, and the rate of change is what is worth watching.
