fixes: The case study. A 100-share order in NVDA was said to have been detected in 2 milliseconds, front-run with a 10,000-share purchase, and sold back 82 cents higher. Three things are wrong with that. A 100-share order in a mega-cap carries no information and is a rounding error against the day's volume. No firm takes on several million dollars of inventory to extract eighty-two dollars. And the story's own numbers do not close: the HFT makes several thousand dollars while the victim loses eighty-two, so whoever is paying, it is not him. The date was impossible too — NVDA split ten-for-one in June 2024 and traded near $135 in October, not $875. Rewritten so the loss stays (it is real and it is the point) and the diagnosis changes: he was sending market orders into fast books and walking up the depth, which needs no villain.

The counterfactual saving. 'December: slippage dropped to $0.18, about $5,600 saved in one month.' That is a guess about trades that did not happen, dressed as a measurement. Removed, with the reason stated, since a lesson that spends five parts teaching scepticism about numbers should not end on one.

'Win rate of 95%+ because they only take statistically favorable trades.' This is a misreading of Virtu's IPO disclosure of one losing DAY in 1,238 trading days. Per trade a market maker loses constantly; the business is the aggregate. Corrected, with the source of the confusion named.

Six invented strategy shares that summed neatly to 100% (market making 40%, latency arb 25%, stat arb 20%, order anticipation 10%, event arb 3%, maker-taker 2%). Nobody outside the firms knows the split. Removed, with the ordering kept because the ordering is the useful part.

Two detection heuristics that describe the ordinary market rather than anything unusual. 'Order cancellation rate: normal 20-40%, HFT active 95-99.9% = quote stuffing or spoofing' — almost all orders are cancelled in every name all day; that is the baseline. 'Odd lots of 17, 83, 241 shares = HFT inventory management' — odd lots are about half of all US equity trades now and a large share come from retail brokers and fractional orders. Both were the lesson-40 error repeated: a reader applying them concludes manipulation is everywhere.

The IEX defence misdescribed the speed bump. The coil delays inbound orders while IEX's own market-data view is not delayed, and that asymmetry protects orders RESTING on the book, not orders crossing the spread — so it does nothing for the marketable order the lesson is telling the reader to protect. Added the part every article omits: at a broker that sells order flow, marketable orders never reach an exchange at all.

'HFT firms see your order 50,000x-200,000x faster than you see theirs' — a category error. Speed determines who reacts first to public information; it gives nobody a private view of your intentions. The wholesaler that sees your order sees it because it is the counterparty.

The institution's $175,000 of slippage on 500,000 TSLA shares was attributed wholly to being anticipated. Most of it is the fund's own market impact, which exists in a market with no HFT in it. 'Firms earn back $100M in 6-18 months', 'market orders cost ~$70/trade in HFT tax', 'IEX saves $500-1,500 over 100 trades' — all invented. 'Patience is free money' — it is not: waiting out a spread during a 2% decline swaps a certain cost for an uncertain one.

The 5 August 2024 open was attributed to quote stuffing. It was a liquidity vacuum from an overnight carry unwind. Also corrected the direction-blind claim that waiting 'saved 1-2%' — true if you were selling, expensive if you were buying.

Fixed 'HFTs detect large institutional orders, front-run them'. Order anticipation is legal and is inference from the tape; front-running means trading ahead of a customer order you were entrusted with.

Removed the claim that HFT firms flood the market with fake orders to manipulate spreads. Quote stuffing and spoofing are prosecuted offences, and the record is against individual proprietary traders and bank desks.
Removed three unmeasured figures: 50-70% of volume, 50,000x faster than retail, and spreads widening 10-50x.
Fixed the objective listing quote stuffing as a detectable tell. Most orders in US equities are cancelled rather than filled, so a vanishing order proves nothing.
strengths: The reframed opening: for retail in a liquid name, HFT is mostly a subsidy
The Flash Crash timeline and the enforcement history
The maker-taker arithmetic, which is correct
All five defences, which are sound execution hygiene independent of the threat model
48-hft-mechanics.summary: Re-read on its current state and raised from C. The reframed opening now says the honest thing -- for a retail trader in a liquid name HFT is mostly a subsidy, and the situations where it is a tax are all things the reader controls -- and the Flash Crash timeline, the enforcement history and the maker-taker arithmetic are all sound. What re-reading found is that the Key Takeaways had not been brought along and still carried the threat model the opening had abandoned. 'HFTs detect large institutional orders, front-run them' misuses a term with a legal meaning: order anticipation is inferring from the tape that a large order is working, it is legal, and front-running means trading ahead of a customer order you were entrusted with. 'HFTs flood market with fake orders to manipulate spreads' is an accusation of criminal conduct against a whole class, which lesson 40 was corrected for making and this one was still making. Three unmeasured figures went with them: 50-70% of volume, 50,000x faster than retail, and spreads widening 10-50x. And the objectives listed quote stuffing as a detectable tell when the great majority of orders are cancelled rather than filled, so a vanishing order proves nothing. The liquidity-withdrawal point survives all of this and is the one that actually costs the reader money: a market maker with no obligation to quote steps back when it cannot price the risk, which is exactly when you want to trade.

fixes: The missing idea, now stated: the imbalance is PUBLISHED. It goes to everyone on the same feed at the same instant, so a good part of the move it implies has already happened by the time you have read the number and clicked. The lesson treated it as though it were private information the reader was lucky to find. It is a regulatory disclosure, and markets absorb disclosures quickly. What remains tradeable is the residual, which is smaller than the headline size suggests. This reframes the whole strategy section honestly: a large imbalance is worth a great deal as a reason not to be positioned against it, and rather less as a reason to be positioned with it.

Five invented hit rates: '65-70% directional' above 5M shares, '70-75%' above 10M, 'the win rate on these setups is 70-75%' in the sizing section, 'roughly 70-75% of the time' in the Quick Wins, and 'about 80% of the time' in a quiz answer. None measured. The lesson's own Part 3 already said 'we are not going to put win rates on either' — so it refused to quote a figure in one section while quoting one in five others. All removed.

The expected-move ladder attached to each imbalance band (0.05-0.15%, 0.15-0.30%, 0.30-0.60%+) was invented. Replaced with what is actually true: the relationship is real in direction and the magnitude depends on the day's resting liquidity, on whether the imbalance gets offset before the print, and on what else is happening in the last ten minutes.

The index-inclusion effect. 'Stocks rally 5-15% from announcement to effective date' comes from research on the 1990s and 2000s. It has shrunk close to zero in recent years, for the obvious reason: everyone knows about it, so it prices on the announcement. Corrected — which makes Strategy 1 much less attractive, honestly so. The Tesla numbers stay because they are correct, and the existing note that Tesla was an outlier at 1.7% index weight is exactly right.
The MOO publication times were Nasdaq's presented as both exchanges'. NYSE begins disseminating opening imbalance information from 8:00 AM, not 9:28.

The MOO quiz answer claimed the order type gives 'no slippage'. An MOO is a market order into the auction and fills at whatever the clearing price is, which on a gap morning can be far from the prior close. What it avoids is walking the book. Corrected, and the invented '$0.05-0.15/share more' removed.

'Do this 4 times before risking real money. If 3/4 worked (75% hit rate), edge validated.' A coin gives three out of four about a third of the time. Raised to twenty, with a clear statement of what twenty does and does not establish. The Quick Wins' 'saves 0.1-0.3% of notional' was also inconsistent with its own worked example, which comes to under a tenth of a percent.

'21 of the 23 trades lost, every one of them held against a 5M-11M share imbalance' — 21 consecutive occasions of a 5M+ imbalance running against him is not a thing that happens. Softened to what he could actually have reconstructed.

Removed 'front-run forced flows for 5-15% gains' from the Key Takeaways. The figure was invented, and positioning ahead of a published rebalance schedule is not front-running -- the schedule being public is precisely why the easy trade stopped working.
Removed 'high-probability directional edge' from the MOC takeaway. The imbalance is public the moment it prints, so whatever edge it carries is being competed for by everyone reading the same feed.
strengths: The auction mechanics, and the block-size context for what counts as a large imbalance
The Tesla example, verified date by date
The spoofing section: an imbalance that shrinks between updates is usually offsetting interest
The case study's ES arithmetic, correct throughout, and its lesson: check the feed before you hold into a close
49-auction-theory-imbalances.summary: Re-read on its current state and raised from B. The mechanics are all sound, the Tesla example is verified date by date, the spoofing section correctly explains why an imbalance that shrinks between updates is usually offsetting interest rather than manipulation, and the case study's ES point-and-dollar arithmetic is right throughout. Two Key Takeaways were carrying claims the rest of the lesson does not support. 'Index rebalancing days -- front-run forced flows for 5-15% gains' had an invented return figure attached to a misused term: the rebalance schedule is published, which is exactly why the easy version of that trade stopped working, and positioning ahead of public information is not front-running. And 'MOC imbalance >5M shares = high-probability directional edge' attaches a probability to something nobody has measured, on data that is public the instant it prints and therefore competed for by everyone reading the same feed. The forced flow is real and worth knowing about; the edge quoted on top of it was not.

fixes: A wrong option letter in the quiz-3 explanation: the text said 2.24% is 'answer B' when B is 4.58% and C is 2.24%. In a lesson whose whole point is arithmetic, a reader who checks would lose confidence in the rest of it.

The composite's after-record ('$151.6K → $178K, +17.4% in 5 months'), which appeared twice. August to December 2024 was a strong market; five months of long exposure measures the market. Replaced with the part that is a property of the rules rather than the outcome: effective risk capped at 1.2%, never more than three correlated positions.

Task 4 of the practice exercise computed each position's loss as the correlated percentage of the move, while ignoring that four of the five stops sit only 1.1-1.9% away. A 2.5-2.9% adverse move does not cost you the correlated percentage on those — it costs the full stop on each, plus slippage. That is a second lesson hiding in the exercise and it is now stated: tight stops do not make a correlated book safer, they make every position hit its maximum on the same morning.

Rachel's example is arithmetically exact ($160,000 of stock at a 4.1% average fill is $6,560) but never mentions that six positions of $26,700 against an $80,000 account is two times gross exposure. She was thinking in risk percentages instead of position sizes, which is precisely how the 4.1% fill becomes an 8.2% account loss. Now stated.

The tail-hedging section repeated lesson 42's error by omission: it recommended long VIX calls without mentioning that VIX options settle against the VIX future for their expiration month, not spot. Spot going 20 to 80 does not take a four-month future with it, and that is the most common way this hedge disappoints. Also added what 0.5-1% per month actually is (6-12% a year of permanent drag) and what a put spread does to a tail hedge (caps the payoff exactly where the crash gets serious).

CVAR appeared in the Key Takeaways but was never defined. Added, with the reason it matters: a portfolio can have a comfortable VAR and a terrifying CVAR, and that shape is exactly what a short-volatility or heavily correlated book looks like.

'Professionals survive 20 losing trades in a row. Retail blows up after 3.' Replaced with the arithmetic, which makes the same point and is true: twenty losses at half a percent costs a tenth of the account; the same streak at five percent, or at half a percent across six positions that are really one, ends it.
50-advanced-risk-management.summary: The best lesson audited in this stretch, and it is not close. It takes one idea — that adding correlated positions buys you almost no diversification — derives the formula for it correctly from portfolio variance, and then applies that formula in about a dozen places without getting it wrong once. Every number I checked came out right: the 0.92 factor at six positions and 0.82 correlation, the 1.18 effective bets, the 0.41 independent-case factor, the 7.5% on the eight-position example, the convergence to √ρ as N grows. An earlier pass had already added the framing that makes it click — nominal risk is the ceiling you hit when every stop fills at once, and correlation decides how close to that ceiling an ordinary bad day sits. The remaining defects were small and specific. The first A in this stretch and an earned one. What distinguishes it is that the lesson does not ask you to believe anything: it hands you a formula, shows you where it comes from, and then works it on real numbers you can check. The case studies exist to illustrate a calculation rather than to sell a system, and both of them are internally consistent to the dollar. The defects I found were a wrong letter, an unremoved after-record, and three places where a true statement could be made more precise — which is a different category of problem from the ones in the four lessons before it. The formula and every application of it. The derivation in the quiz-3 answer, which correctly goes from portfolio variance to the working form. The Callum and Rachel case studies, whose dollar arithmetic is right throughout. The heat-limit table with its existing caveat that the 10-15% figures belong to institutional desks. Emma's exercise, including the correlation-matrix averaging over all ten unique pairs. The position-sizing quiz, whose every figure checks out.
50-advanced-risk-management.title: Your Positions Are More Correlated Than You Think

fixes: The heat cap said three different things in one lesson. Part 3 correctly sets the retail limit at 6% and explicitly names 10-15% as an institutional-desk figure. The Pro Tip dashboard immediately below it then shows 10.2% heat with a green tick and instructs the reader to wait only above 15%; the practice exercise says a 14.75% book sits 'inside a 15% cap'; and the closing checklist asks whether heat is under 'your 10-15% cap'. Worse, the dashboard produced its 10.2% by putting each strategy's Kelly fraction in the heat column — the exact conflation the paragraph above it warns against. Rebuilt the dashboard so the middle column is risk per open trade and the total is 4.3%, moved every cap reference to 6%, and named the allocation-versus-heat confusion in the text.

Lisa's recovery after-record — 'Switched to 1/4 Kelly (4.2%). Results: $71K to $111K (+56%) in 6 months, max DD -12%' — carried in both the case study and its quiz answer. Removed from both. What replaces it is the part that was always the real evidence: run the identical six-loss streak at 4.2% and 0.958^6 = 0.773 takes $192.5K to $149K instead of $64K. That $85K is arithmetic on a streak that happened. The +56% was a forecast about trades that did not.

The prop-trader worked example did not add up. Old sizing at 2% gave +$140K/year (+28%); new sizing at 3% was reported as +$224K/year (+45%), with the text saying return and drawdown both scaled by roughly 1.5x. The drawdown did (15% to 22%), but 140 x 1.5 is 210, not 224. Corrected to +$210K (+42%), which is what the lesson's own stated scaling requires.

The Three Pillars table put 'Kelly Criterion adjusted for edge strength (5-15% for proven edges)' in the Institutional column. No institution risks 5-15% of the fund on a position; the figure is a retail quarter-Kelly number wearing an institutional label. Replaced with what institutions actually do differently, which is recompute the fraction as the estimate of the edge moves.

Ed Thorp's 'roughly 20% a year for two decades', quoted twice. Princeton/Newport ran 1969-1988 at about 15% net to investors and around 19% gross. The 20% is the gross figure presented without the label. Corrected in both places, with the distinction stated, because a lesson about compounding should not quote the number an investor did not compound at.

The practice exercise closed with 'If the edges hold, expect roughly 15-25% CAGR with 12-18% peak-to-trough drawdowns' — a forward projection invented from three estimated edges. Removed, and replaced with the collision the exercise had accidentally built: quarter Kelly on three real edges asks for 14.75% of the account and the retail heat cap says 6%, so scale all three by 0.41 and size to the smaller constraint.

Equity-curve position sizing was presented as pure upside. Added what it is — a trend-following overlay on your own equity curve — and what it costs: it pays when results cluster and bleeds when they merely alternate, because then you are small into every recovery and large into every drawdown.

Fixed the Key Takeaway that capped portfolio heat at 10-15%, contradicting the section it summarises. Retail cap is 6%; 10-15% is an institutional-desk limit assuming hedging and balance-sheet depth a retail account does not have.
Removed 'increase size to Kelly %' from the Signal Pilot section. That is full Kelly, and a confirmation does not turn an estimated win rate into a known one.

Reframed the equity-curve sizing rule. A 20-day equity average is a smaller sample than the hundred trades this lesson has just shown cannot pin down a win rate; on independent trades the rule adds no expectancy and keeps you small into the recovery. It is worth having only if drawdowns change how you trade.

The seven-loss-streak arithmetic, checked: 0.4^7 is about 0.16%, or once in roughly 600 trades
The Portfolio Heat worked example, including the distinction between heat and allocated capital
The correlation adjustment: correlated strategies are the same bet
51-portfolio-construction-kelly.summary: Re-read on its current state and raised from B. The estimation-error argument added in the earlier pass is the strongest thing on the page and is rarely made anywhere: Kelly assumes p and b are known, they are estimated from a finite sample, and on the lesson's own 60%/1.67 example a hundred trades puts the true rate somewhere near 50-70%, which returns 36% at one end and 20% at the other. Since overbetting destroys growth faster than underbetting costs, the error is asymmetric -- a second and better reason for fractional Kelly than the variance argument. The Portfolio Heat section was corrected to the retail 6% cap with the 10-15% figure identified as an institutional-desk limit. What re-reading found is that the Key Takeaway still printed the 10-15% cap, contradicting the section it summarises. Two more: the Signal Pilot section told the reader to 'increase size to Kelly %' on a confirmation, which is full Kelly, four screens from the part explaining that nobody should; and the equity-curve rule was presented as a pure benefit when a 20-day equity average is a smaller sample than the hundred trades the lesson has just finished saying cannot pin down a win rate. On independent trades it adds no expectancy and keeps you small through the recovery. It is now framed as what it actually is -- worth having if drawdowns change how you trade, which is a statement about the trader.

fixes: The central rule was arithmetically impossible. 'When you see 50M shares bought in 10 minutes, institutions are ACCUMULATING' appeared six times — in the case study result line, the missed-signals list, the breaking-point quote, the recovery rule, the quiz option and the quiz answer. SPY trades roughly 70-90 million shares across all venues in an entire ordinary day. Fifty million in ten minutes is most of a session. The recovery rule also asked for 'sweeps >10M shares', which is not what a sweep is. Rewritten throughout with the real scale stated: a large SPY block is a few hundred thousand shares, a large single-name block is tens of thousands, and if a number quoted at you would be most of the day's volume, the number is wrong.

'Magnet behavior: price gravitates toward VWAP throughout the day (institutions pull it back)' — a causal claim about an arithmetic property. VWAP is the volume-weighted average of every price so far today, so on a directionless day price is mechanically near its own average most of the time. On a trend day price sits on one side of VWAP from open to close and never returns, and no amount of algo activity drags it across. Corrected, along with the practice exercise's 'on 3 or more days out of 5, price will typically revert at least three or four times' and the Quick Win's 'you will find SPY returning to VWAP three to five times' — both invented counts, and both false on precisely the days that matter.

The block-print table inferred intent from a print. Every block has two sides: a 200,000-share print is one institution buying and another selling at a price both accepted, and the print does not say which was the eager one. Added the honest reading before the table — a buy printed above the day's average price means the buyer took worse-than-average execution to get filled, which is weak evidence of urgency, not evidence of conviction or of being right.

'Standalone icebergs can be spoofs' contradicted the lesson's own quiz answer twenty screens later ('icebergs refresh instantly; spoofs get pulled before filling'). A spoof is cancelled before it fills; an iceberg is defined by continuing to fill. Replaced with the alternative explanation that actually competes: a market maker absorbing retail sell orders and hedging elsewhere produces an identical tape and has no directional opinion at all.

DIX described as a 'smart money sentiment' gauge, which contradicts Lesson 36's correction that most off-exchange share volume is wholesaler internalisation of retail orders rather than institutions crossing in dark pools. Reframed as what it is: buying pressure in a stream that is heavily retail, with some documented relationship to forward returns but not the mechanism usually claimed for it.

Ryan's composite after-record ('$99K to $162K, +64% in 7 months, 69% win rate'), carried in the case study and repeated in Quick Win 3 with the flourish 'those two numbers — 28% fading it, 69% joining it — are the whole argument'. Removed from both; the disaster record and the 19-of-67 count stay, because those are counts of trades that happened.

'DIX divergences are high-probability reversal signals' in an exercise whose entire purpose is to have the reader measure that frequency for themselves, and a 'win rate boost' claim on a worked trade.
Fixed 'Block trades show intent: above VWAP = bullish, below = bearish'. Blocks show that size changed hands and where; the tape carries no side, so intent is not readable from the print.

Corrected the DIX takeaway, which described it as measuring dark pool flow and told the reader to follow it. DIX is reconstructed from short-sale data precisely because prints are unsigned, and the takeaway immediately below already walks the instruction back.
Fixed the VWAP takeaway, which said price gravitates to it flatly, where the lesson's own objective promises to teach when it does and when it does not.

The five-step iceberg detection walkthrough and its absorption-ratio arithmetic
All three worked trades, whose figures check out
The closing takeaway, which states the reliable form of the rule as the negative one
52-institutional-order-flow.summary: Re-read on its current state and raised from B. The two best sections -- how a VWAP algo behaves around fair value and how to read an iceberg off the tape -- are correct, concrete and hard to find explained this well anywhere else, and all three worked trades check out arithmetically. The closing takeaway had already been corrected to the honest version: trade with the flow not because institutions are right, since the other side of every one of these prints is also an institution, but because size moving one way creates hedging and follow-on execution, and the reliable form of the rule is the negative one. Three takeaways above it had not been brought into line. 'Block trades show intent: above VWAP = bullish, below = bearish' asserts a side the tape does not carry -- whether a print above VWAP was a motivated buyer or a seller filling one is not on the screen. 'DIX measures dark pool flow: above 45% = institutions buying (follow them!)' both misdescribes DIX, which is reconstructed from short-sale data precisely because prints are unsigned, and issues an instruction the takeaway directly beneath it walks back. And the VWAP line said price gravitates to it, where the lesson's own objective promises to teach when it does and does not.

fixes: The regime score adds volatility and trend as if they were one axis. ADX above 25 scores +1 for trending, ATR above 1.5x scores +1 for volatile, BB Width above 8% scores +1 for expanded — so a chaotic news-driven session scores +3 before the VWAP and volume terms are counted, reading 'strong trending, trade pullbacks and breakouts' on exactly the day the lesson elsewhere says to sit out. The practice exercise then bolts on a 'High Volatility override' to undo it, which is an admission the single number does not work. Split into a trend score and a volatility reading kept beside it, with both required before sizing up.

Both composites carried complete after-records. Sarah: '6 trades, 83% WR, recovered $4,200 ... recovered $11,800 ... 3-month summary: recovered $16,000, account $51,700 ... 17 trades, 0 in the wrong regime, regime match 100%.' Marcus: 'Feb +$2.2K, Mar 73% WR +$14.6K, Apr 78% WR +$11.8K, 3-month recovery +$28,640 (+27.6%), final $132K.' Both removed. Both replaced with the countable change, which was always the real evidence: Sarah went from 38 trades in eight weeks to 17 in twelve; Marcus took 4 trades in a range month where the comparable stretch before had produced 15.

The headline statistic was four trades. 'She had a 75% win rate when ADX > 25 (4 trades: 3W/1L)' was repeated as '75% win rate in trends' in the closing summary, the Key Takeaways, the Quick Wins and the quiz answer. Three out of four is not a win rate. Rewritten to put the weight where it belongs: 7 winners in 34 trades losing $41,700 is a result luck does not produce, and it establishes the negative claim, which is the useful one.

Both stories were dated onto quarters that contradict them. Sarah's reflection claims the market trended 80% of the time in Q4 2023 and only 10% of the time in Q1 2024 — but Q1 2024 was one of the strongest and steadiest first quarters on record for US equities, not a chop. Marcus's disaster is dated Nov 2023 to Jan 2024 with 'SPY chopping $440-460 for 11 weeks', which is the sharpest two-month rally in years described as a range. Dates removed from both, with the reason stated in the text: date a composite and someone will pull up the chart.

The deeper statistical problem, which neither case study acknowledged and which is now stated in three places: regimes arrive in blocks of weeks, so 'my trending trades' and 'my ranging trades' are two consecutive stretches of one account. Any strategy compared across a good period and a bad period shows this gap whether or not the regime caused it. Marcus's 18-of-24 against 12-of-45 is a real gap and worth acting on; it is not a controlled test of ADX, and the lesson now says so.

The practice exercise told the reader its own answer before they measured. 'You'll likely find 60-80% win rate when matches, 20-40% when doesn't' — removed. fixes: The central mechanical error, and the most valuable correction in this lesson: a fair value gap is not a gap. The three-candle shape means candle 1's high sits below candle 3's low — but every price in that range printed, during candle 2, and somebody was filled at each of them. What the pattern marks is displacement: a move fast enough that the bars either side do not overlap. That is real and worth watching. It is not untraded price, and no auction principle requires a return to it. The lesson's auction analogy ('the auctioneer skipped $520, so someone yells about it') was doing the wrong work entirely, and the genuinely untraded gaps — overnight and across halts — got named for the first time.

The FVG fill statistics table (70-80% same session, 85-90% within 24 hours, 95%+ within three days), quoted again in the Aha Moment and again in the Key Takeaways. No such figure exists on an inspectable sample, and the base rate destroys it anyway: an intraday FVG is a zone a few cents wide near the current price, and price revisits almost any such zone within a day. Worse, the gaps that matter most — the wide ones left by a trend day — are precisely the ones that do not fill. Replaced with a counting exercise that records gap width, time to touch, whether it held the midpoint, and the day type, because that last column is where the answer actually lives.

Emma's case study contradicted its own moral. Her review split $71,000 into $7,014 of execution cost and $64,000 of directional loss — and the lesson then declared 'auction illiteracy' the fatal mistake, with a quiz question marking that answer correct. Nine dollars in ten came from being wrong about direction. Question and options rewritten so the correct answer is the split itself: separate what your ideas cost from what your fills cost, then work on whichever is bigger.

The slippage figures were off by a factor of thirty to sixty. '$0.30-0.60/share midday' in SPY and QQQ, stated five times. Both quote a one-cent spread for essentially the whole session and a retail order rests inside it. Half-dollar slippage on 200 shares of SPY comes from market orders or from a far less liquid instrument, not from the hour. Corrected with the diagnosis that actually applies, plus a Quick Win that has the reader measure their own.

'Exit at 3:58 PM MOC', instructed four times. The MOC cut-off is 3:50 PM on both NYSE and Nasdaq; after that new MOC orders are rejected. The instruction cannot be followed. Corrected, keeping what is true — the closing auction is routinely the largest single print of the day.

'Enter ONLY at 9:31-9:35 AM' — the open has the highest volume and also the widest spreads, the most volatility and the most adverse selection, and the rule contradicts the lesson's own Part 1, since you cannot read an opening range that does not exist yet. Removed, and the execution advice reduced to the part that actually does the work at retail size: use limits, not market orders.

'Above POC = expensive, below POC = cheap', stated in the section heading, the Key Takeaways and the practice exercise. The POC is where the most volume traded in a window you chose. In an uptrend price is above yesterday's POC every day and keeps going, and a trader reading that as expensive shorts the whole trend. Reframed as a map of where two-sided trade should be expected, with the day type from Part 1 deciding whether it is tradable.

'Performance is typically 65-70%+ at the exact VAH/VAL touch', 'trade FVG fills with 70%+ accuracy', 'Success criteria: 7+ out of 10' (replaced with the base-rate point), 'your expectancy skyrockets', 'floor trader-level mastery', 'you're in the top 5% of traders', and the invented winning outcome attached to the five-way confluence setup.
Fixed the Pro Move, which called a rejection at the 50% fill a high probability trade -- the exact claim the FVG Statistics section three screens below refuses to quote.

Rewrote the practice exercise, which told the reader that 50% fills that hold are the highest-probability reversal trades. That hands over the conclusion before the exercise that was supposed to test it; it now asks whether the distinction is visible in the reader's own data at all.

strengths: The central table is exact rather than simulated, and the method is given in enough detail to reproduce it in twenty lines. At a 45% win rate an eight-loss streak inside 200 trades is a 53% event; 93 traders in 100 running that same profitable system meet a six-loss streak.

Separates the statistical question from the structural one and is honest that the statistical one usually cannot be answered: 143 trades to establish a total collapse, 571 to catch a halving, 2,284 to catch a 25% degradation. It then refuses the lazy conclusion, naming explicitly that undetectability cuts both ways and a halved edge will keep paying badly for years.

The composite case is load-bearing rather than decorative: the error is not the size cut but that the size cut was unplanned, which undersized the recovery trades and converted a normal 11R drawdown into a longer one the trader then read as confirmation.
The Signal Pilot section opens by stating that no indicator can answer the question the lesson is about, and confines the tools to the structural half.
55-variance-or-broken-edge.summary: New lesson, written to fill the largest gap in the curriculum: 86 lessons taught how to build an edge, measure where returns came from and survive drawdowns by sizing, and none told the reader how to decide whether a losing run is inside their own distribution or evidence the edge is dead. The spine is that a losing streak is not a data point until it exceeds what the reader's own win rate produces routinely, and every number that supports it is computed rather than asserted: the streak table is exact dynamic programming, the drawdown distribution states its simulation count and seed, and the detection sample sizes fall out of the noise-to-signal ratio of a single trade. The load-bearing artefact is a table the reader recomputes for their own win rate, which is what separates this from a lesson about variance.
55-variance-or-broken-edge.title: Is Your Edge Gone, Or Is This Just Variance?

fixes: Two hundred and sixty lines of after-record removed: Act 3's month-by-month Q3-Q4 table (+$32,900), Act 4's 2024 strategy-by-strategy table (+$112,200 across 128 trades), the before-and-after comparison table, 'Eric's Current Reality' with its $134K annualised pace, and the 'Total Impact of VIX Education' summary ending in 'ROI on VIX education: Infinite'. The dated VIX levels did not happen. 'Feb 24, 2023, VIX 29.4' — VIX was about 21.7 that day. 'May 4, 2023, VIX 24.3' — about 18.3. 'VIX hit 31 on Nov 3' 2023 — VIX was about 14.9, and it had not been near 31 at any point that autumn. Only the March 2023 credit-scare figure was close. All dates removed rather than corrected, per the pattern used elsewhere in this audit.

The lesson never mentioned that you cannot buy the VIX, then told the reader to trade its reversion. Added the mechanics that decide whether being right pays: every vehicle tracking VIX holds futures, and during a spike the front future already trades far below spot because the reversion is priced. And the trap in the lesson's own recommended expression — buying SPY calls during a spike is long delta AND long vega at the most expensive implied volatility of the cycle, so the vol crush works against the option while the direction works for it. Shares, or a call spread, express the same view without paying for the volatility you expect to fall.

'VIX > 30 reverts to 15-18 within 2-4 weeks' — contradicted by this lesson's own COVID case study, which correctly notes VIX stayed above 30 until early June 2020, fourteen weeks. 2008 held above 30 from September to April. Those are the episodes that make VIX spike in the first place and the ones that kill a reversion trade sized for a quick unwind. Corrected in the Key Takeaways, the practice exercise and the new Act 3.

The 'VIX < 15 = 75% size' row was presented as the same kind of rule as the others, but it runs the opposite way: low VIX means narrower ranges, so sizing off your stop already gives a larger share count for the same dollar risk. Relabelled as what it is — a discretionary tail-risk overlay, defensible but not implied by the volatility itself.

'Whale trades (10,000+ contracts) can predict directional moves 6-24 hours ahead' in the Key Takeaways — the same false lead-time claim corrected in Lessons 37 and 51. Replaced with what a large print does establish: dealers must hedge, which is real flow, and it happens immediately, not hours later.

'Checking one number prevents 30-50% of bad trades', 'trading high-VIX costs you 2-4x more per loss' generalised from 10 trades, 'Target 1: VIX return to 20 (usually +5-8% SPY move)' with its invented VIX-to-index conversion, 'one of the highest-probability mean reversion trades in markets', and the closing 'you just learned what separates professionals from amateurs'.

Rewrote the learning objectives, which told the reader to fade the fear above VIX 30 and buy the reversion in SPY -- both contradicted by this lesson's own Key Takeaways, which give fourteen weeks in 2020 and over six months in 2008.

Fixed the Real Talk box, which called VIX a gauge that predicts chaos before it happens. VIX is the price the market is currently paying for insurance; it says what is being priced now, not what is coming.

Removed 'when VIX hits 30+, it's screaming BUY THE DIP' from Part 1, and replaced it with what the level actually tells you: daily moves of roughly 1.9%, which is a statement about how wide the stop needs to be.
Fixed the Aha Moment's 'when fear subsides (it always does), VIX reverts to 15-18'. The question is never whether it comes down but whether you are still solvent when it does.

57-algorithmic-execution.summary: Re-read on its current state and raised from C. 'First/last 15 minutes of session = widest spreads' is only half right, and the halves are different problems: the opening genuinely has the widest spreads, because the overnight gap is being priced and market makers quote defensively until the day shows itself, but the close does not -- the closing auction concentrates enormous volume and spreads there are usually tight. What the close has is speed, so a market order into it is more likely to be run over than spread-gouged. Conflating the two sends the reader looking for the wrong cost. And the practice exercise still promised to 'reduce slippage by 30-50%', an invented target on an audit whose whole point is that you do not know the answer before you run it.

The section labelled 'risk parity' was inverse-volatility weighting. True risk parity equalises the risk contributions computed from the full covariance matrix and generally has no closed form.

63-performance-attribution.summary: Re-read on its current state and raised from B. The invented after-record is gone, the Sortino claim is corrected, and the selection effect is now named where it matters: choosing the winner from several six-month samples is choosing the maximum of several noisy estimates. What re-reading found is that the Key Takeaways commit that same error twice at finer grain. 'Time-of-day matters: avoid low-WR windows' is the strategy-level mistake applied to hours -- slice a year of trades into hourly buckets and one will look terrible by chance alone, so dropping it is choosing the minimum of several noisy estimates. The fix is to look for a mechanism first and check the record second. 'Review monthly: identify what works, eliminate what doesn't' has the same shape, and the honest version is asymmetric: attribution is reliable for finding what to cut and unreliable for finding what to scale, because stopping a strategy costs an opportunity while scaling the wrong one costs capital. 75-multi-timeframe-confluence.title: Multi-Timeframe Confluence: The Highest-Probability Setups

fixes: Removed the composite's before-and-after profit framing ('-$8,400 + $34,050 = $25,650 after learning intermarket analysis') and the $300K position it rested on. The SPX path from 4,238 on 1 November to 4,719 on 15 December is real and checkable, and it stays; what one trader made from it is not observable and has gone.

Renamed the section from its dollar figure to what the case actually demonstrates, and added the two caveats: the signal missed the 27 October low by 121 points, about a fifth of the move, and the measurable benefit is the fourteen entries it would have prevented rather than the one it produced.
76-intermarket-analysis-advanced.summary: The October 2023 lead-lag walkthrough is the best-researched passage in the tier: every SPX close, DXY level and 10-year yield in the table is a real public print, and the lesson uses them to demolish its own field's favourite claim — copper was flat through the SPX low and gave ground in January while SPX kept going, so on that move copper did not lead, yields and credit did. It goes on to correct the Dow Theory record, the gold-versus-real-yields relationship (real yields were deeply negative through 2021 and gold finished down), and the folklore that credit always leads equities. One composite after-record fixed. All 11 locales rebuilt clean.

fixes: No content defects found. Retitled the long detailed action block, which shared a heading with the standard short closing block and rendered "Quick Wins for Tomorrow" twice on the page.
77-behavioral-finance-psychology.summary: The strongest lesson in the curriculum on evidence handling. It cites the Brazilian day-trading study rather than folklore, caveats the Kahneman-Tversky 2:1 loss-aversion ratio as varying by person and context, names the Van Tharp '60/30/10' split as a number with no measurement behind it and keeps only the ordering, flags the Dunning-Kruger curve as partly a regression artefact, and gives the actual Dawson and Reid finding rather than the version usually quoted. The four-bias composite is built on real TSLA, GME and COIN closes from February to May 2021 — every date and price checks out, and the arithmetic ties to the dollar at nine separate points, ending at 77 times the loss his own plan called for. The same duplicated heading was found and fixed in four other lessons by a repo-wide scan (39, 41, 65, 71). All 11 locales rebuilt clean.
77-behavioral-finance-psychology.title: Behavioral Finance: Your Brain Is The Enemy

fixes: Named the contradiction between the opening composite and the lesson's own Phase 3 success criterion: the criterion is 15-25% annually net of everything, and the example averaged 34.8% for four consecutive years with no losing year. Added a callout resolving it in the criterion's favour, cross-referenced to lesson 62's arithmetic on 34% a year.
Removed the composite's Sharpe track ("1.1 rising to 1.6" across four years), which is noise given a one-year Sharpe carries a standard error near 1.4.

Replaced the Sharpe gates in the capital-growth phases: 50-100 trades cannot distinguish a Sharpe of 1.0 from zero, and a twelve-month Sharpe is not much better, so Phase 1 now gates on expectancy and drawdown and Phase 2 on twelve months of profit plus a drawdown sat through without changing size.
Retitled the section away from its dollar figure, and pointed the reader at the two parts of the block that do not depend on how the market behaved: the cost line and the deposit split.
78-building-trading-business.summary: The tax section is the most careful in the curriculum: an LLC on its own changes nothing about your tax, an S-Corp gives no relief from self-employment tax because capital gains were never subject to it, trader tax status is the thing that matters and has no statutory test, the 475 election is due in mid-April for a year you cannot see yet, and a $10,000 deduction at a 32% rate saves $3,200 rather than $10,000. Part 4's aside — a $150,000 account returning 20% makes $30,000, and you can draw a living from it or compound it, not both — is the honest sentence most career content omits. The four-year composite was the weak point. Evidence held at B because the year-by-year return path remains an invented sequence; it is now explicitly framed as optimistic and contradicted in place rather than presented as the expected outcome. All 11 locales rebuilt clean.
78-building-trading-business.title: Building a Trading Business: From Hobby to Profession

fixes: Corrected the headline claim that the account fell $78,000, or -49%. It did not: about $8,000 was realised trading loss and roughly $70,000 was opportunity cost, and forgone gains do not come out of a balance. Added the general rule this exposes — a case study that adds opportunity cost to realised losses and reports the total as a drawdown is wrong in the direction that always flatters the story.

Removed the recovery's after-record ($82K to $137K, +67% in five months, 71% win rate), keeping the change that can be counted: 34 trades in the next five months against 8 in the previous five, on the same setups. Five months is not a sample, and quoting a return there would be doing the thing the corrected paragraph above it just took apart.
Trimmed the case-study heading and the trader quotation to match.
79-real-time-market-analysis.summary: A capstone that mostly earns the name. It states its own honest limit in the learning objectives — synthesising several streams buys context and a veto, not a measurable percentage — and repeats that discipline in each Quick Win ('what it gives you is a written reason to pass'). The quiz explanations are the best in the tier, especially question 2: three green pre-market numbers read as agreement is exactly the trap, because a genuine risk-on rally has bonds falling. Tyler's case had two arithmetic problems, now fixed. All 11 locales rebuilt clean.
79-real-time-market-analysis.title: Real-Time Market Analysis: Synthesis in Action

fixes: Clarified the one ambiguous number in the confirmation checklist: "2.3x average volume (150M vs 65M avg)" compared a fifteen-minute breakout candle against a daily average, and SPY does not trade 150 million shares in a quarter of an hour. The bar is now stated as the breakout candle against the median volume of that same fifteen-minute slot over the last twenty sessions, with the session total kept as a separate check.
80-live-trading-case-studies.summary: Four worked trades including a loss, each with sizing, management and a post-mortem, and the R-multiple arithmetic ties in every one. The best passage is the Maya section, which does what almost no trading content does: it says that scoring a pattern on the winners you selected it from tells you nothing, then re-scores all 218 trades by pattern so each carries its full record — and still calls 17, 12 and 14 trades small samples. The quiz answers are unusually careful (a dark pool print establishes size but not intent; volume is contemporaneous with price rather than lagging), and the takeaways state twice that no honest failure rate exists for the multi-timeframe check. The Maya after-record (47% to 73% over three months) is left standing because the lesson deflates it in place twice, naming both the sample size and the market's share of the change. All 11 locales rebuilt clean.
80-live-trading-case-studies.title: Live Trading Case Studies: Theory Meets Reality

fixes: Gave the Jenna case the same treatment the Emma case already had: 33 trades carries a standard error on the win rate of about eight points, six months is one regime, and the market gets a vote in any six-month figure. What the style change demonstrably bought her is not in the P&L — it is the first stretch she finished without overriding her own rules.
Qualified the "Sharpe ratio > 1.0" pass criterion in the validation framework: a Sharpe estimated from two years of data carries a standard error around 1.0, so it is a floor and never a ranking.
81-building-your-edge.summary: The three-dimension frame is the right one and the verdicts on it are honest: informational edge is bought with infrastructure you do not have, analytical edge is where retail can compete, behavioural edge costs nothing. The Emma case is a model of how to present a discovered edge — it names the selection effect out loud ('a number found by picking out the setup that had already worked, which is exactly why the next six months are the part that counts') and then refuses to annualise the six months that follow. Tom's case correctly attributes his loss to latency, missed exits and revenge trades rather than to the strategy. Two smaller items brought into line. All 11 locales rebuilt clean.
81-building-your-edge.title: Building Your Trading Edge: Personalized Strategy Development

fixes: Corrected the strategy description: credit spreads and iron condors are defined-risk structures, not "undefined risk". Every position he held had a capped maximum loss, which is what makes the case worth reading — he lost half an account without a single undefined-risk trade in it.

Re-diagnosed the failure by division. $143,000 across 18 positions is about $7,900 of maximum loss each on a $285,000 account, or 2.8% per position; eighteen open at once is 50% of the account at simultaneous maximum loss, which is exactly the -50% he took, because in a correlated crash every short SPY structure resolves the same way at the same time. That is a Layer 2 failure, not a Layer 1 one — each trade was sized like a professional, the book was not.

Reordered the "what went wrong" list to put the aggregate heat limit first, and noted that fixing the VIX filter, the daily loss cap, the circuit breaker and the size reduction without fixing that one would have reduced this loss rather than prevented it.

Removed the recovery after-record ($142K to $267K, +88% over 18 months) and replaced it with the bound the rules actually give you, which is checkable in advance: the same eighteen positions under a 5% aggregate heat limit cap the crash at $14,250 rather than $143,000. Also noted that the eighteen months after March 2020 were among the friendliest ever recorded for selling equity premium.
82-professional-risk-systems.summary: The five-layer stack is the right structure and the layers are genuinely distinct: per-trade risk, aggregate heat, daily circuit breaker, drawdown threshold, tail protection. Brian's case is the best material in the lesson once the arithmetic is done on it, and doing that arithmetic turned out to change what the case teaches. All 11 locales rebuilt clean.
82-professional-risk-systems.title: Professional Risk Management Systems

fixes: Corrected the Tesla inclusion case, which claimed the stock "did not make a new high after inclusion". It did: TSLA closed 2020 at $705, took out the 18 December high on the last day of the year, and ran to roughly $880 by late January. Added what that means for the takeaway — the sell-the-news dip was real and brief, and a reader treating inclusion day as the top would have shorted into a further 27%. The reliable part of the pattern is the run-up between announcement and inclusion.

Corrected the merger-arb hedge. Shorting the acquirer hedges a stock-for-stock deal, where you receive shares and want to lock the ratio; MSFT/ATVI was all cash, and in an all-cash deal there is nothing to short. The arb desk's advantage there is position sizing against an estimated break probability, not a hedge.
83-institutional-trading-strategies.summary: The MSFT/ATVI merger-arb walkthrough is exact — announcement price, the widening through the FTC suit and the CMA block, the restructuring and the October 2023 close all check out, and both annualised returns compute correctly. The dark-pool section corrects the number most trading content gets wrong (40-50% of volume trades off-exchange, but true dark pools are nearer 10-15%; the rest is retail internalisation). Two factual errors fixed. Evidence held at B: the strategies are described accurately but several are presented as replicable at retail scale in more detail than the "what you cannot replicate" section later walks back. All 11 locales rebuilt clean.
83-institutional-trading-strategies.title: Institutional Trading Strategies: The Professional Playbook

fixes: Removed the "EVERY month green for 12+ months" precondition and its two repetitions. A strategy running a profit factor of 1.5 produces losing months routinely — that is what a profit factor of 1.5 means — so demanding twelve consecutive green months selects for a lucky year rather than a durable edge, and it is the criterion most likely to keep a ready trader waiting or push an unready one into massaging the record. The lesson contradicted itself on this: its own case study attributes Amy's months nine and ten to variance. The bar is now twelve months of aggregate profit over a documented sample of 300+ trades, with the losing months visible in it.
84-career-pathways-trading.summary: The most honest career lesson in the curriculum. It replaces the '95% fail' folklore with the Brazilian and Taiwanese research and says why the research is more damning than the round number; it names the prop-firm incentive problem out loud (the firm earns on failed evaluations) and tells the reader to plan on being in the long tail; and its income table ends on the sentence the genre never writes — the returns are a function of account size, not skill, and a brilliant 30% year on $50,000 is $15,000. One internal contradiction fixed. All 11 locales rebuilt clean.
84-career-pathways-trading.title: Career Pathways in Trading: Building a Professional Future

fixes: Removed a checklist item the lesson's own plan cannot satisfy: it demanded a 20+ page trading plan while the Week 1 deliverable specifies 10-15 pages. Replaced the page count with the actual test — a plan is finished when someone else could trade it without asking you a question.

Qualified the "backtest Sharpe above 1.0" checklist item in line with the rest of the curriculum: a Sharpe from a few years of data carries a standard error near 1.0, so it is a floor rather than a score, and expectancy in R over the same 100 trades is the number to act on.
85-final-capstone-project.summary: A real capstone with real deliverables, a costed six-week plan whose hours actually add to 55, and quiz explanations that catch the two errors readers most often make: a 50-setup backtest is a provisional read rather than permission to size up, and average R-multiple per trade IS expectancy in R, so tracking both is tracking one metric twice. Dan's numbers are internally consistent — 55% at 1.7:1 gives a profit factor of 2.08 and an expectancy of +0.49R, both as quoted — and his Phase 1 block ends on the right note: at $79 of risk a trade, eighteen trades cannot make you rich and cannot hurt you either. All 11 locales rebuilt clean.
85-final-capstone-project.title: Final Capstone Project: Your Trading System Blueprint

fixes: Removed the one unhedged after-record on the page (Daniel's +$38,700 over six months after switching strategies) and said why: six months of results on a new strategy measures the market he traded into, not the review. The review's contribution is entirely on the loss side, and that part is measurable.

Replaced the quarterly red flag "Sharpe ratio dropped below 1.0 for 2+ consecutive quarters". A Sharpe computed on three months of trading carries a standard error well above 1.0, so that rule fires on a healthy strategy about as often as on a broken one. The decision now rests on win rate, payoff ratio and expectancy over the last 50 trades.
Changed the annual goal-setting takeaway from Sharpe targets to what the trader controls: rule adherence, sample size and review cadence.
86-ongoing-learning-community.summary: The right lesson to end on, and it does two things almost no course does. It says out loud that its own regime table stops where its author's data stopped, and makes extending it the exercise. And the Chris case refuses to report a Sharpe on a 28-trade sample, saying so explicitly, while keeping the claim that survives: the specific mistake stopped. The Daniel case is genuinely elegant once the counterfactual is done properly — a review does not stop the decay, it stops you paying for it for another fifteen months, which turns $62,400 into about $10,000. All 11 locales rebuilt clean. This completes the per-lesson audit: 82 of 82.
